speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
report, concurrence in which is now sought, comes from the Committee on Agriculture which met about five days ago. It reads:
That without delaying investigation by this committee as to the advisability of the reestablishment of the Canada Wheat Board, the matter of the constitutionality of such re-establishment be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada and that every effort be made to secure decision at an early date.
There had been, in this connection, referred to the Committtee on Agriculture the subject of handling the wheat of this country, and although the reference was not correctly or, at least, not adequately made, the intention was, no doubt, to ask the committee to consider the subject in three aspects: First, whether the Wheat Board, with all its old powers and duties,

should be re-established; or, second, whether there should be established a Government organization to handle and dispose of wheat committed to it by the voluntary act of the producers; or, third, whether the whole question should be left to what was described as co-operative action on the part of the producers themselves. The reason I say that the matter was intended to be referred in that form is because, in that form, the intended reference was described by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his speech on the Address. Consequently, though the words of commitment were narrow, I apprehend that a third report recommending a fuller reference will be adopted and the reference widened accordingly. It will be recalled that the former Wheat Board, that is the Wheat Board, established by Order in Council of July 31, 1919, which Order in Council was continued by this House very shortly afterwards in the same year and later on confirmed by legislation in the spring of last year, had very ample powers in a sense, indeed, monopolistic powers. It had certain control over the elevator system of our country and over the transportation of grain committed to it, and certain priorities and extraordinary rights which at the time it was deemed wise to repose in the board. That Wheat Board was discontinued-or rather the time that was originally given to it as its term of life expired, and consequently, no act of discontinuance was essential. It handled the wheat crop of 1919, and having so disposed of its duties, it ceased to exist. In the spring of 1920, there being some doubt at that time as to what would be the condition of the buying market in -Europe, and also as to what would be the policy of the United States, whether that country would remain in control, in some form or another, of its wheat marketing, or whether it would revert to the old marketing conditions, Parliament, on the advice of the government of the day, passed legislation empowering such government, if in its opinion conditions so demanded, to restore or to continue the Wheat Board as it had been established, for the purpose of taking in hand the crop of 1920. The government of the day did not exercise that power. European countries were no longer purchasing, as they had been doing, through the single agency of the British Government, which in turn acted through the British Wheat Commission, but were buying through agencies-although Government agencies-active in competition the one

Wheat Board
with the other. Besides, the United States Government had abandoned all attempts at wheat control, or marketing control of any description as regards grain, reverting instead to the old market conditions. In view of these facts the late Dominion government exercising its judgment did not reestablish the board.
Some time after, a grain inquiry commission was instituted under the Inquiries Act, upon complaint, which had become very general, that there were abuses in connection with the handling of the grain trade of western Canada. That commission was enjoined; the Order in Council establishing it was challenged, and that Order in Council was declared invalid by a judge of the King's Bench of Manitoba. Subsequently, upon appeal-and in all modesty I call this to the attention of the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), whom, had he not shown the contrary in his speech on the Address, one would have expected to be already aware of the fact-the' validity of the Order in Council was established, the powers of the Government to pass it were confirmed. This matter was decided by the Court of Appeal of Manitoba.
In view of the evidence adduced before that commission, and in view of the very evident condition of dissatisfaction throughout the West over the whole question of purchase, storage, financing and disposal of its grain, I, in the late campaign, proposed an alternative, namely, the second alternative recited by the Prime Minister in his speech on the Address: that is to say, the establishment, not of a board with compulsory powers, not of a single agency excluding all other agencies of sale, but of a board with ample powers to receive, move, finance, and finally sell, and distribute the proceeds of, all grain committed to its charge by the will of the producer. I am not proposing to discuss now the merits of this plan or of any of the plans to which I have made allusion; I do not purpose even to discuss whether or not the late government took the right course in this regard. That question does not arise on the motion of my hon. friend the Chairman of the Committee on Agriculture (Mr. Kay). But a review of the facts such as I have given is necessary in order that what I have to say anent this motion may be the better understood. The demand for the old Wheat Board that was made has been received by the committee who, proceeding to deal with the question, have made a report to the House that while they were considering the wisdom of its re-establishment- whether or not differing in personnel-the Government refer to the Supreme Court of Canada the question as to the power of this Parliament to establish such a board.
Now, I submit to the House that if we concur in this report it is going to be impossible to meet the situation for the coming summer. I do not pretend to judge the full measure of those who demand the establishment of the old Wheat Board with all its powers, but I do say that there is i a very strong body of support for that proposal. Of its numbers, its strength, and its right to be heard before a committee of this House and this House itself, there is no question. But there are those among its numbers-I do not know what proportion, but I should say a substantial proportion, I think I can say the majority-who, while they urge strongly, under what they describe as abnormal conditions existing now, their right to the advantage of the old Wheat Board, with all the means of disposal it afforded, during this year and perhaps next year, at any rate while these conditions prevail; nevertheless do not ask that the board be established as a permanent institution. They insist only that it be put into operation to take care of the situation during this period of abnormalcy. Their insistence is mainly that it be established for the purpose of taking care of the wheat crop of this year. There are, I do not know how many, but doubtless a considerable number, who would favour the establishment of the board permanently. But however great their numbers may be, the number of those who want it, not on a permanent but on a temporary basis, is far greater. Of that there can be no question. Consequently this House, before it takes any step that will put it practically out of its power to comply with this demand, must very carefully decide, yes or no, thereto. Whether the demand is right or not, of its very nature it calls for a decision by this Parliament at an early date.
What will happen if this resolution carries? This House will have instructed the Government of the day to submit, to the Supreme Court of Canada a definite question, namely: Is it within the competence of the Parliament of Canada to reestablish the Wheat Board with the powers vested in it under the Order in Council of July 31, 1919, as confirmed by Parliament? Be it noted, there is no question at issue
Wheat Board

at all as to the powers of the Governor in Council. The committee realized that fully in this report. There is no doubt at all that the Governor in Council has no such powers now ;[DOT] but the question is whether the Parliament of Canada has such powers. It was the Parliament of Canada that acted before. Parliament confirmed the action of the government, because the government had to act, if it took any action at all, before Parliament met, or there would have been no time to take in hand the 1919 crop. Parliament confirmed the government's action, and the question is: Has Parliament the right to do what Parliament actually did in the special session of 1919? If that question is submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, assuming, as I do, that every effort will be made by the Government to prosecute the suit to a decision-I will not be asked to assume any more, indeed I think I am liberal enough when I assume that much-is there any substantial hope that we shall get a decision from the Supreme Court of Canada, upon which we can act, within such time as will enable us to dispose of the question at this session? Who are entitled to be heard before that tribunal? Well, the Government of Canada will be heard. They will undoubtedly be there by counsel, endeavouring, I presume, to establish the power of this Parliament. I would also expect that some, possibly all, of the provinces of Confederation, whether unitedly or separately, would appear before the Supreme Court on the issue. I would expect the Grain Exchange to appear before the court. Possibly the Grain Exchange would come individually, or perhaps forty companies strong, as it has been known to come before the courts of the country before. How many companies of the Grain Exchange are going to be heard? Can they be denied a hearing? I would expect, as well, the millers' association, and perhaps individual milling companies would want to be heard. I would expect that the railway companies would be there, and possibly our banks as well. It is a matter that interests in an important degree many great fields of enterprise in this country. There would be inevitably a warring clamour of interests before the court; and when any one of those interests could establish a prima facie case for postponement, how could the court deny a postponement? I know of interests that would have a lot to gain by a postponement;

I know of interests who would desire postponement. In the hands of able lawyers, I do not know of any kind of case that is more easily made out, than a case for postponement, and I for one would despair, were I acting for the Government in such a connection, of any early decision, no matter how assiduous and vigorous was my conduct of the case.
But, suppose we get a decision, is there anything to prevent an appeal to the Privy Council? There will be one, you may be sure, if the case goes in favour of our powers. And if there is such an appeal who is going to take care of the 1922 crop of wheat?
But, beyond that, suppose my conjecture as to what is going to occur on the argument of this case before the Supreme Court is wrong, and we find lawyers, opposed perhaps from forty different angles, all in agreement to press the case to a decision in order that Parliament may act in the light of that decision; suppose that happens-which would be a miracle-what then? We get a decision. Is the decision going to be of great practical value? Is it going to be of a character that would enable Parliament to act in a practical way? I do not think it can be. In the original statute twenty-seven different powers were given to the Wheat Board; starting with A, B, C, continuing through the whole length of the alphabet, and still one more. There were multiplied duties besides imposed upon the Wheat Board. The Supreme Court would have the power to go into one and all of those powers and duties. But I do not know that it would do so. It might say: Here is a power that we find the Parliament of Canada cannot repose in the board; it is ultra vires; therefore we need not decide the other points at all.
But suppose the court went on and decided one and all, supposing they did everything, assume, indeed, a set of facts the most adverse to my contention possible, suppose they deal with A, B, C, and so on all through the list. What then? Assume they decide that we are ultra vires as to the whole twenty-seven, it might still be that by a modification, perhaps an unimportant modification, of each one we could come well within the powers of this Parliament, and at the same time establish a board so armed and equipped that it could substantially meet the ambitions and desires of those who seek this method of the disposal of their grain. The judgment, when it comes, shall not in all prob-

Wheat Board.
ability be such to enable us to act on it in a practical way.
To sum up what I have argued so far. First: follow this course and you are plunged into the caldron of litigation, from which in all human probability you will not emerge until it is too late for you to act with much value this session. Second: though there may be harmony, and all go smoothly to an early verdict, the judgment alone will not be of such a final, definitive and detailed character as to be what we want in building the fabric of legislation.
Then I am asked: What are we to do? Well, I would advise Parliament to say to the committee: Go back and do what has always been done,-take the advice of the law officers of the Crown. When you decide just what you want, the principle you want to follow, the body you want to establish, the powers you would like to give it, go and sit beside the law officers and ask them: How far in that direction can we go and be as safe as any one can be from the threat of injunction? There is no difficulty about taking that course. I know it may be said that possibly after you take their advice you may be faced with an injunction afterwards. Why, so you may be, whatever you do. But in the light of the decisions that have so far been handed down, particularly in the light of the decision a few months ago by the Court of Appeal of Manitoba, I do not think there would be any great difficulty on the part of the law officers of the Crown in so framing legislation that we would be tolerably, if not wholly, safe from the danger of successful injunction at the instance of any litigant.

speechtext:
Might I interrupt my
right hon. friend? Is he arguing on the basis that the enactment by this Parliament would confer all the powers that the original Wheat Board had?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
I am afraid I have not been fully understood. I say, suppose the committee decides: We would like the Wheat Board; but if we cannot have the Wheat Board with all its powers, we would like to get as close to those powers as we are sure we can safely go. Then let them express that desire through the Government to the Justice Department, and have the Justice Department frame legislation which will in the opinion of its law officers reach as far as this Parliament can go. That seems to me the practical and sensible course to take.
Let it be remembered that there has been expressed some doubt as to the power of
this Parliament in regard to the entire handling of the grain trade. We may be in some danger there even as we sit now. But the fact is this, the grain trade has become of such a character, it is so interprovincial, it is so broadly Canadian, that whatever may be the constitution of this country, that trade must be under the control of legislation enacted by this Parliament,-under the control of federal authority. And if there is successful attack that goes to the root of our power in this matter, I for one would be prepared to support legislation which would address the Imperial Parliament in terms requesting an enabling amendment of our constitution.
I express here no opinion one way or the other on the merits of these different proposals; I am not arguing for the Wheat Board, nor against it; I am not arguing for a voluntary government board, nor against it; nor am I advocating abandoning the whole difficulty in a spirit of laissez faire to what is called "cooperation." For the present it seems to me the sensible step to take is to let the committee decide after hearing evidence and arguments what they believe would be best in the interest of the whole country, and let them express their decision in a resolution. Let the committee as well go, through the Minister of Justice, to the law officers of the Crown and arrive as closely as may be done at the expression in statutory form of powers within the competence of Parliament which in the judgment of that committee should be vested in the board which they think this Parliament should create. That is the alternative course that I propose.
I only want to impress this thought upon the committee before I sit down. You never can get wholly out of danger of litigation, no matter what you do. But take the course proposed in this matter from the government side and you will wave good-bye to any wheat board established by any act of Parliament this session. I do not know of any way by which a decision could come in time to be of any value except by general concurrence adverse to our powers. In a word, take the course proposed in the motion and you ditch the whole question; you abandon it; you are done with it. That, in my judgment, would be the practical result. I urge on the contrary that the other course be followed; and I therefore move:
That the said report be not concurred in but be referred back to the Committee on Agriculture for further consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter underlying the reference to the Committee on Agriculture, the second report of which has brought about this discussion, is one of the very greatest importance. There is no question what the opinion of western Canada is-[DOT] not only of the agricultural portions of that part of the Dominion, but of its business interests as well-as to the urgency of this matter of the re-establishment of the Canada Wheat Board. I could, if this were the proper occasion, give many reasons why it is in the national interest that the Wheat Board should be re-established along the lines advocated by the memorandum submitted by the Canadian Council of Agriculture to the Government, and later, referred to the Committee on Agriculture.
The conditions in the West have been of an extraordinary character. I am not overstating the fact when I say that an overwhelming majority of the farmers of western Canada conducted their business last year at a loss. One reason why they have had such a poor return for their year's labour was the manner in which their grain was marketed under the exceptional conditions prevailing throughout the world. We cannot throw into the markets of Winnipeg, forty or fifty or sixty million bushels of wheat a month and expect the markets of the world to absorb it as freely as it is offered for sale without a considerable depression in prices. That constitutes one of the strongest reasons why action along the line of re-establishment of the Canada Wheat Board should be taken.
I am, therefore, quite in accord with what my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) has said as to the urgency of this matter. In fact, I wish to express my delight at the interest he is manifesting in it. I recall that back in 1920 the government of the day was empowered to re-establish the Wheat Board under act of this Parliament, and one of the first things my right hon.	friend	did	after he	became prime
Minister was to announce to the country that no wheat board would be re-established,-and the need for it then was fully as great as it is to-day.
There is, apparently, a doubt whether this Parliament has the power to pass legislation enabling the Wheat Board to function,	as it	did	function,	when it marketed the crop of 1919. My right hon.	friend	has refrained from givingan opinion	upon that	question; probably he has a doubt in his own mind whether Parliament has that power. Being

a layman and unfamiliar with the tenets of the law, I certainly would not venture an opinion on the point. But I know that the view is held by eminent legal gentlemen that a doubt exists whether Parliament has the power to pass legislation creating a Wheat Board with compulsory powers, that is, with powers to pass regulations and orders compelling farmers to sell their grain -and market it through the agencies created by the board. The position taken in the committee was inspired by the desire to clear up that doubt, if possible, before any such legislation was passed. The report of the committee suggests that, without delaying an investigation by the committee of the merits of this method of marketing the grain, steps should be taken to secure from the Supreme Court of Canada at as early a day as possible a decision as to the power of Parliament in the matter. I think that view was expressed by the committee in order that, if possible, the legal doubt hanging round the thing might be cleared up.
My right hon. friend argues that there would be a great deal of delay in getting such an opinion from the Supreme Court.
, That might be; I am not familiar with the regulations governing the Supreme Court and I am not in a position to say with what despatch they could consider this matter and come to a decision upon it. I have it in mind, however, that in the summer of 1917, when a question arose over the powers vested in the Government under the Military Service Act in the city of Calgary-

I stand corrected-it was in 1918. As to the powers vested in the Government under the Military Service Act, a question arose in Calgary which necessitated a submission to the Supreme Court. If I recall the circumstances correctly, habeas corpus proceedings were taken to release a young conscript who had been imprisoned for violation of some of the provisions of the conscription law, and the Supreme Court of Alberta sustained the injunction. In that case it was necessary for the government to determine quickly just what the legal status of the conscription law was, and I recall that steps were taken at once to have a stated case placed before the Supreme Court, and the court gave its decision within a week of submitting the case. It does seem to me that it would be possible, if the Govern-

Wheat Board
ment used despatch, to get a decision from the Supreme Court as to the powers of Parliament in this matter in a very short time. I do not think there is any one, either in this House or outside, who approaches this question with the honest desire to get the best possible conditions established for the marketing of grain, who would wish to see the Wheat Board re-established, and then find it, after it had started operations, hung up in the air and unable to continue its work.
Legal gentlemen in private conversation with me have also cited the case of the Board of Commerce. This act creating the Board of Commerce was passed by the preceding parliament in 1919, conferring very wide powers on the board in the matter of the regulation of trade. I think it will be in the mind of every member of this House that that legislation was contested in the courts and that the Board of Commerce was restrained and put out of business as a result of the decision of the Privy Council.
Those are some of the considerations that moved me in my consideration of this matter. I recognized, and the committee recognized, the urgency of the case by urging that the Government should secure a decision from the Supreme Court as quickly as possible.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, Who, I am free to confess at once, has had eminent legal experience, seems to be of the opinion that a decision could not be secured from the Supreme Court in any reasonable length of time, and he suggests instead that this matter should be referred to the law officers of the Crown.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
The Supreme Court
might give an adverse opinion at an early date, if it was the general opinion of the court that Parliament had not this power, but in my judgment certainly we would not get a favourable opinion in time to deal with the matter this session.

speechtext:
That is a matter, again, in which I am upon rather unfamiliar ground. I would be of the opinion that if a majority of the Supreme Court gave a decision in favour of the contention that Parliament had the power to create this board, that would be ample warrant for the Government going ahead and establishing it; but in any case I have no fault to find with the suggestion of my right hon. friend that the matter be referred to the law officers of the Crown. The only point in respect to that is that there would perhaps be a doubt as to the conclusiveness of an opinion handed down by the law officers of the Crown.
I want to repeat, this is a matter of urgent importance and one on which action should not be delayed a moment longer than is absolutely necessary. I do not know what action the committee might take, assuming that Parliament had the power to pass legislation creating the board, but I do say this: I think the committee whose reports we are considering were perfectly well intentioned in the matter when they desired to ascertain the exact legal position, and at the same time have their inquiry proceed, as indeed it is proceeding now, as to whether the re-establishment of the board would be a desirable course to take.

speechtext: For the benefit of those of us who do not belong to the Agricultural Committee, perhaps my hon. friend would explain whether the doubt with regard to the power of Parliament bears on the primary power of Parliament to establish a Wheat Board or is the doubt merely with regard to the compulsory feature that is mentioned?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: The doubt exists, I think, in the minds of the committee, as to the power of Parliament to pass legislation creating a board with compulsory powers such as the powers the board had that was established in 1919.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: It is the compulsory feature as to which there is a doubt?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: The compulsory feature. It is not necessary to have action from Parliament, I take it, for the creation of a voluntary pool, but there is no doubt that if such action were necessary Parliament has the power to pass legislation creating a voluntary pool, such as my right hon. friend advocated during the election. But that is more a matter for action by the Government than by this Parliament.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: Is it the view of the committee that the creation of a Wheat Board with powers less than those of the original Wheat Board would be satisfactory to the interests in the West that are affected? In other words, would a Wheat Board without compulsory powers be satisfactory?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
I think I may say that such a board would not be satisfactory. The memorandum of the Council of Agriculture
Wheat Board

which gave rise to this question asks specifically for one thing and one thing only, and that is the re-establishment of the Canada Wheat Board with all the powers it had in 1919. That is what the memorandum asks for, and that is what we are considering in the matter.
I do not know that any harm could come from a further reference to the committee, as my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition suggests. It might be that the collective wisdom of the committee could proceed a little further in considering this question, although I must confess I am rather doubtful of what results could be obtained from such a reference back. However, it might be productive of good results, and is a step that I think could be adopted by the House.
The main thing I want to emphasize is the urgency of action in this matter. If the doubt could be cleared up quickly as to whether Parliament has the power to reestablish this board, I think it would be distinctly in the national interests that that be done. It may be that an opinion from the law officers of the Crown, as my right hon. friend suggests, would carry with it a greater degree of eonelusiveness in the public mind than seems to me now probable or likely, but in any case I see no reason why that action should not be taken by the Government. Let the Government, through the law officers of the Crown or through the Supreme Court, find out what the powers of Parliament are in this matter, and in the meantime let the committee proceed with its inquiry and bring in a report based on all the evidence that is placed before it. I think it would be of great service if the powers of Parliament in this matter were determined as quickly as possible.
In dlosing, I simply wish to say that this is a matter of very great urgency, and I trust that it will receive the consideration of this House from that angle, and that angle alone.
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (Calgary West): Mr. Speaker, I venture to address the House on this question, because in my judgment it is one of the pressing problems of the hour in so far at least as the western part of Canada is concerned. Let me at the outset state quite frankly that I am in favour of the re-establishment of the Wheat Board. I am not prepared to say that I favour that as a permanent arrangement, but I certainly am in favour of it as a means of taking care of this year's crop and perhaps of next year's
l Mr. Crerar.]
crop as well. Now, I am not by any means alone in that contention. I understand that the United Farmers in the province of Alberta in convention assembled have practically unanimously favoured the creation of this board, and the farmers of Saskatchewan, and I believe also the farmers of Manitoba, with equal unanimity have concurred in the views of those of Alberta. If, therefore, the Wheat Board is to be of any value for this particular year it is necessary and urgent that every effort be made by this Parliament to ascertain whether or not the reappointment of that board is in the interest of this country.
I endorse the remarks of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) on the subject of referring this matter to the Supreme Court of Canada. It is true, as the hon. member for Marquette has stated, that in the military case, the Lewis case, which arose 1 believe in the city of Calgary, a decision was given by the Supreme Court in one week; but hon. riiembers will realize that that case is entirely different from this, because there the accused himself was anxious to have it determined whether or not his liberty should be taken away from him in the particular manner complained of. In the present instance reference to the Court could only be made after a very careful study of the questions involved; and of course this would take considerable time, because the constitutional questions involved are serious and extremely difficult. Not only that, but the Supreme Court must necessarily give ample opportunity for the provincial governments, and the various interests concerned, to appear and to prepare their cases and to present arguments before it. Now what I suggest, Mr. Speaker, is this: It is absolutely physically impossible to have the Supreme Court of Canada give a decision in this pai'-ticular case in anything like the limited period suggested by the hon. member for Marquette; it seems to me the result would be that this matter would be long drawn out. A litigant-and perhaps there would be many of them, and also various conflicting interests, before the Supreme Court -who felt dissatisfied with the decision of the court would have the right of appeal to the Privy Council, and then the matter could not possibly be determined until long after the 1922 crop had been cut and harvested. Now my suggestion is simply this -and I will not detain the House longer- that the matter should go back to the committee with instructions that they

Wheat Board
should consult the legal staff of the House -and I think everybody will agree that the legal staff are indeed able, in connection with the particular constitutional problems involved-and ascertain whether or not valid legislation can be passed, or whether in the event of legislation being passed, enabling legislation might also be passed by the various provincial legislatures, the converse of what has been done in connection with liquor legislation. I simply make the suggestion because I seriously contend that the adoption of the report of the committee means that we simply embalm the Wheat Board in litigation long before it is born.

I can see no reason why under the circumstances, they should not have this privilege.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the matter is finally dealt with I want to touch on one feature of the case which has not yet been alluded to.
With a great deal that the 4 p.m. leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for West Calgary, and the, hon. member for Marquette have had to say I most heartily agree, but there are some other matters that perhaps should be brought to the attention of the House. The illustration of the Board of Commerce has been mentioned and it has been pointed out that should this legislation be put into operation, and part of the crop be taken off, an injunction might then be served upon the board with very serious consequences. That might be the case but I submit that although for many years the Canada Grain Act has been in question, yet because it has been of inestimable value to the nation as a whole and because its operation was a matter of national good, no one has yet contested the validity of that act. If the Wheat Board should be established and the fact of its being for the general good of the country recognized by this Parliament, no one will seriously question the proceedings of the board while it is operating temporarily.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the Canada Grain Act is now being attacked in the Manitoba courts?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is or not. If such is the case then I am slightly at fault in that regard. The other matter to which I wish to refer has reference to the widening of the powers of the Committee on Agriculture. I for one am absolutely free to say that I would encourage the widest possible investigation into anything that would promise relief to the conditions in western Canada; but in this particular instance I would like to call attention to the fact that there is no demand for anything else but the Wheat Board; and as was stated in answer to a question by an hon. member opposite a moment ago, nothing but the reestablishment of the Wheat Board, with powers almost identical with, or similar to, the powers of the old board would satisfy the West at this time, in my opinion. So far as my own constituents are concerned, and to them I owe a duty in this matter, I must say that I cannot support anything but the re-establishment of a board with powers similar to those of the old board. I stand most decidedly in favour of that policy.
Now I do not think at this time it is proper to go into a discussion as to the value of the board. That can very properly be done in committee, but when this matter is being referred back to committee for consideration I would also submit that the committee be advised to follow this procedure: First, to consider the recommendation of the Canadian Council of Agriculture. When that is absolutely disposed of, one way or the other, let the committee take up question number two, and afterwards question number three. Because, I do not think we should close the doors to an investigation into any matter that may be productive of good. Nevertheless, the chief question before the committee, and the one that was referred thereto by this House for a decision, is the one question of the appointment of the Canada Wheat Board.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
The question raised in this discussion, as to the legality of the proposed Wheat Board, involves the most interesting constitutional point and one which I think, in the interests of the people of the West, as indeed of the whole country, ought to be settled along lines that would leave no doubt as to the power of this Parliament to deal
Wheat Board

with the subject. The suggestion that the determination of the constitutionality of such legislation should be deferred-a suggestion made by the leader of the Opposition-does not seem to me to be one which would be in the interest of the gentlemen from the West or of their constituents. A matter of so much importance as this ought to be determined by that court in Canada which has the power of saying what the constitutional rights of this Parliament and the various legislatures are. It might be proper to enable this committee to go to the limit of what seems to be the powers they have under the advice of the law officers of the Crown; but I think those who are very much interested in this matter would be well advised if they would join in urging that the Government should take steps for the early and final solution of the legal powers involved.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) referred to the fact that a decision had been given not long ago as to the power of this Parliament to constitute the Board of Commerce. That decision was one upon which the members of the Supreme Court of Canada divided equally. The judgment of Mr. Justice Duff upon that subject was strong and clear; and, looking at it, as I have since this discussion came up, I find that he laid down principles which, if they are followed by the courts in dealing with this subject, would make it clear that this Parliament has no power to constitute a board similar to the Wheat Board of 1919. His judgment was con-1 firmed by the Privy Council in a deliverance so clear that every hon. member, who is acquainted with legal matters and who follows this case, will realize that this Privy Council decision is one of the most important decisions given of late years. Let me submit this statement by Mr. Justice Duff as regards the question of the power of this Parliament in dealing with matters of this kind. He states:
The creation of an authority endowed with such powers of fixing the terms of contracts in relation to specific articles appears to involve an interpretation of the words, "regulation of trade and commerce," much more comprehensive than anything contemplated by the decisions and Judgments referred to above, I have indicated the principle which in my opinion is deducible from Parson's Case (1), namely, that section 91-(2) does not authorize an enactment by the Dominion Parliament regulating in each of the provinces the terms of the contracts of a particular business or trade, for the reason (put very broadly) that such legislation involves an interposition in the transactions of individuals in the provinces,

within the sphere of property and civil rights and local undertakings not contemplated by section 91-(2).
Further, he states:
I cannot discover any principle consistent with these conclusions, upon which an enactment delegating to a commission the authority to regulate the terms of particular contracts of individual traders in a specified commodity according to the views of the Board as to what may be fair between the individual trader and the public in each transaction, can be sustained as an exercise of that power;
That language of Mr. Justice Duff which was confirmed in terms by the Privy Council, seems to me to lay down principles which materially interfere with the theory that a Wheat Board can be legally constituted. As I say, the decision given by the Lords of the Privy Council on this matter went further than most lawyers anticipated that it would have gone. It was held previously that the fact that section 91 of the British North America Act gave to this Parliament the right to deal with the regulation of trade and commerce, carried with it certain ancillary powers, which enabled this Parliament to go further and deal with matters which might fall within the purview of property and civil rights, subjects within the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures. But this declares that the powers which this Parliament assumed in order to pass the Board of Commerce Act and to give that board power to deal with certain matters which might arise in certain provinces of the Dominion, were not ancillary to the regulation of trade and commerce and were beyond the power of this Parliament. It seems to me, in view of this decision, hon. gentlemen who, I know, are interested in this subject and are anxious to see the business and trade of this country, especially in the great West, put upon a solid' footing, would be well advised if they saw to it that steps were taken, at as early a date as possible, to have a decision by the Supreme Court as to just what this Parliament can do in regard to this Wheat Board.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not purposed discussing this matter, and I will speak of only one or two questions that have been presented. It has been urged that it is beyond the powers of this Parliament to pass legislation compelling individuals to sell their property to any particular board. I apprehend that is the law; I apprehend it will always be the law. But is such a power necessary to the enactment of legislation that will 'bring

Wheat Board
about that which we seek and that which is asked for by the people of western Canada ? What is the situation to-day? The people of western Canada are not asking this Parliament to regulate the trade of selling their wheat to neighbours; they are asking this Parliament to determine how their wheat shall be marketed in the markets of the world, how it shall be handled by the great transportation companies of our country, what agencies shall engage in the commerce of handling the wheat of western Canada. Those powers have been vested in governmental authority for years. Every bushel of wheat that has gone out of western Canada since the enactment of the Grain Act, has gone out under the regulation of laws passed by this Parliament, and it will continue to do so. We ask that that power be placed in the hands of a government board, and that power may be properly placed there. Under our constitution, trade and commerce are within the purview of this Parliament. That has been the case with our Grain Act. It is suggested that the constitutionality of the Grain Act has been challenged. Possibly, there may be features of the Grain Act that are unconstitutional; but are they necessary features? I think not. The only question that I have heard raised was whether the provision in regard to the forfeiture of certain overages to the Government was constitutional. Probably it is not. I do not apprehend that the Government has a right to take private property without paying for it. But is it necessary that such a power be put into the hands of such a board? Most certainly not. The question is raised whether the tight to issue a license is not a provincial right. It is a provincial right as to three particular kinds of licenses - keeping a hotel, acting as an auctioneer, or running a saloon; such licenses must be issued by the province. But the elevator business is not auctioneering, nor hotel-keeping, nor running a saloon; and when the provision covers those three powers, does it not withhold the balance of the power? This matter should go hack to the committee. I believe that when this legislation is proposed, it will be attacked, and if we present a case to the .Supreme Court any blackleg 'lawyer, who represents some curbstone broker, can hold it up for two or three years. In the meantime, where shall we be in the West? I ask that this matter go back to the committee and that we have legislation drawn that will effect the pur-50
pose which we seek. It may not be couched exactly in the language of the old bill, but it must be such as will give the people the relief they desire and that we need most sorely.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: On the question of enlarging the powers of the Committee, I would emphasize the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). We in western Canada are not asking for any voluntary wheat pool or any other system of marketing grains, except under such conditions as prevailed under the old Wheat Board. If the Committee has extra powers conferred upon it, I would suggest that it confine its activities, as far as possible, to looking into the question of a compulsory Wheat Board.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Supporting the action of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), I would point out that if the report goes back to the committee and the law officers of the Crown are able to produce an act that in their judgment will be constitutional, we shall be that much further ahead than if we* appealed to the Supreme Court. Even if a Wheat Board is appointed by Parliament and an attack is made upon it, we shall certainly be as far ahead as, if not further than, if we submitted a stated case ro the Supreme Court of Canada. If Parliament puts through legislation and it is subject to attack in the courts, it will reveal to those who are anxious to have the Wheat Board established, the persons, firms or interests that are trying to frustrate that desire. And that, I submit, would be something worth while discovering. I notice that my hon. friends, who know more about farming than I do, do not want a permanent Wheat Board. I have said in this House before that one thing which, in my judgment, Parliament ought to do is to prevent, as far as it can, any speculation in foodstuffs. I may be somewhat straight-laced, or possibly I do not understand some particular phases of the question; but to me it seems almost a crime to permit such speculation in food as raises the price to the consumer and reduces the return to the producer. I have always thought that a permanent Wheat Board that would get the most that was possible for the producer, and at the same time protect the consumer, was legislation that we might very well pass in this House. As I say, my hon. friends from the prairies do not seem to believe in a permanent Wheat Board, and I con-



Armaments
cede to them a greater knowledge of the case than I can possibly have. But they would gain more, in a matter of great urgency, by having some measure passed by Parliament, after being properly considered by the officers of the Crown, than if they submitted the question to the Supreme Court.

Amendment agreed to.
Motion as amended agreed to.

speechtext: On the motion of Hon. G. P. Graham (Minister of Militia and Defence) Bill No. 14 to amend the Salaries Act and the Senate and the House of Commons Act, was read the third time and passed.
Sir LOMER GOUIN (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 25 to amend the Penitentiary Act.
The explanation of the Minister of Justice was almost negligibly brief on the introduction of this bill. Perhaps he will give us a better explanation now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I said in introducing this bill, when a prisoner is sent to a penitentiary, the warden cannot receive him if he is suffering from an infectious disease, and there is no provision in the statute to authorize the return of such prisoner to the jail whence he came or to any other institution, to be treated. We propose by the amendment to remedy that omission in the statute so that in such a case the prisoner may be sent back to the provincial authorities for treatment and returned to the penitentiary when cured.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
On section 1-prisoner may be kept in penitentiary, etc., until necessary documents, including a certificate of health, are delivered to warden:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 45 of the Penitentiaries Act reads:
Whenever a prisoner is ordered by competent authority to be conveyed to any penitentiary from any other penitentiary, or from a reformatory prison, or from a jail, there shall be delivered to <the warden of the penitentiary receiving such prisoner, together with all other necessary documents, a certificate signed by the medical officer of the institution from which
50i
prisoner has been taken, and countersigned by the official in charge of the penitentiary, reformatory or jail from which such prisoner has been taken, declaring that such prisoner is free from any putrid, infectious or contagious disease, and that he is fit to be removed.
Then, section 46:
The warden shall receive into the penitentiary every convict legally certified to him as sentenced to imprisonment therein, unless certified by the surgeon of the penitentiary to be suffering from a dangerously infectious or contagious disease, and shall there detain him, subject to the rules, regulations and discipline thereof, until the term for which he has been sentenced is completed, or until he is otherwise legally discharged.
These are the sections proposed to be amended by the bill. The amendments are found to be necessary by the provincial authorities.
I notice that the amendment makes no mention of a hospital or similar institution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, the prisoner has to be sent back to the jail from which he came. No special hospital is provided.
But suppose the jail has no infirmary, for example, in connection with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He can be treated in the jail. There is a department for such purposes in almost every jail in the country, I think.

When I had the honour of acting as Solicitor General, a number of cases arose in the Department of Justice upon which this amendment would have a direct bearing. The difficulty was that in some of the jails in Ontario, and in many similar institutions in Nova Scotia, there was no proper arrangement for the custody of prisoners suffering from contagious diseases. The matter was brought to the attention of the law departments of the various provinces on more than one occasion, but they did not seem to recognize it as their duty to provide suitable quarters for such cases. There is no doubt that hardship and difficulty resulted to prisoners because of this condition. I can recall several cases in Ontario where prisoners had contagious diseases of a very virulent type, and the placing of these men in the ordinary penitentiaries would be just ground for objection on the part of the other convicts. On the other hand, there is no adequate facilities in the local jails to take care of these prisoners, and what is to be done in the circumstances is a rather difficult problem.
Penitentiary Act

Men who are the victims of a loathsome disease are sometimes sentenced by judges to penitentiary terms. They are first confined in the local jail, and orders for their removal to the penitentiary arrive in due course. But they should be accompanied by a certificate as to health before being admitted into the penitentiary, otherwise trouble might ensue among the other convicts. If they are returned to the local jail, the same difficulty may arise there, or the unfortunate man may receive no adequate treatment. In a number of cases while I was in that department, persons suffering from certain diseases we~e treated in the local hospital under guard. Frequently we had to release prisoners for the purpose of having serious operations performed on them; they were released on parole or under guard and after recovery were brought back to the penitentiary. But some new system should be evolved. The authorities in charge of the provincial jails should be compelled to see that some proper treatment is accorded to prisoners who are so afflicted. Personally, I think the amendment proposed by the minister is a proper one and ought to be adopted. But it does bring up that broader question: what are we going to do with the unfortunate criminal who is condemned by a court of law and does not receive proper treatment in our jails? If he is treated in the jail, what are you going to do about the other prisoners who are there and who are liable to the contagion?

Not only are the prisoners-the diseased men as well as the others-to be considered in this matter; it affects the public generally. If a number of prisoners take ill, say, with scarlet fever, diphtheria, or any other contagious disease, the expense to the country is increased. I do not know whether another clause could be added to the amendment to provide for this. I notice that the minister shakes his head; apparently it cannot be done. Now, I have been in some of these jails-though not as a prisoner- and I know that often there are no facili-ities for caring for men afflicted in this way. I suggest to the minister that if something could be done to provide for these cases it would be in the interests not only of the prisoners concerned, but of the public as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are now legislating in respect of penitentiaries, which are under the jurisdiction of the federal 
government. We have no power to legislate for the provincial jails. As to the cases my hon. friend mentions of contagious diseases in certain jails, I do not know much about the other provinces, but I had the honour of being Attorney General of Quebec for some fifteen years, and I know that when such cases arose there the prisoners were sent to a hospital and returned to the jail after treatment. If the matter is to be dealt with as regards the provincial jails, it must be done by the provinces themselves. As to the penitentiaries, we do the best we can. We are legislating to give full protection to the prisoners, and I have reason to believe that even under the law as we had it before, full protection was given them. We are providing here that the provincial authorities may take a prisoner suffering from a contagious disease and treat him in a jail or some hospital if that is found necessary.

I agree with the minister that we are legislating in regard to our own penitentiaries, but we must remember this-that the judges who administer our criminal law, which we pass, convict these men, and sentence them to the penitentiary. The penitentiary is under our jurisdiction and if we pass this act and a man suffering from a contagious disease is sentenced to a penitentiary and that sentence is not carried out by reason of his disease, he is readmitted to the county jail, which has no adequate means of taking care of him. I know county jails in the province of Ontario, and apart from those in the larger cities I do not know of one that has any facilities at all for caring for convicts suffering from a contagious disease. We pass the criminal law; we appoint the judges who administer it; our appointees sentence the convict to the penitentiary, and now we are passing a law which says that unless the convict is in good health he cannot be admitted to the penitentiary; he must go back to the county jail whence he came, where there are no proper facilities for looking after him. I agree that we have no authority over these county jails. That is the difficulty of the situation, and in correspondence I have had on that matter when we have suggested that the county jail should be put into a condition to attend to these prisoners we have been practically told to mind our own business. There is the difficulty, and it is that I wish to point out.

Penitentiary Act

There is another
point involved that has not been touched upon, and that is that if a prisoner is sentenced to serve a term in a federal prison, and is afterwards under this legislation sent back to a county jail, the cost of maintaining him is thrown back on- the county, when by right it should fall on the Dominion. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

There seems to be a
lack of provision as to who is to pay for the medical attendance necessary. There is something also in the draftsmanship of this bill which requires a little attention. It proposes to amend section 46 of the present act by adding at the end the following:
Provided that a convict, if certified by the surgeon to be suffering in manner aforesaid, may remain and be kept in his former custody until his condition shall In the opinion of the surgeon justify withdrawal of the certificate.
Now you have the sentence of the court, which says that he shall go to the penitentiary. Then, under this provision, if the convict is suffering from a contagious disease, the sentence is suspended, and the will of the surgeon is substituted for everything else. Suppose the surgeon finds him incurable- and he may well be possessed of a disease which is readily communicable and is not curable-apparently then he would remain in the jail for life at the cost of the municipality, which has to maintain the jail. The municipality would have to pay for his board and medical attendance. Of course, no such result is contemplated, but it seems to me there is a deficiency in the structure of the Act in not providing for a resumption of the jurisdiction of the court which sentenced the convict.
I may also add to what has been said on the subject of the unfitness of the county jails. There is not in the province of New Brunswick one jail in which it would be humane to keep a prisoner who is suffering. In the city of St. John-I do not say the jail there is the best-the jail is utterly inadequate. There are no proper accommodations, and it would only be inflicting unnecessary cruelty on a man under sentence to compel him to be looked after in such a place. I trust that this matter will receive more consideration. I am satisfied that every one in the House wants to accomplish the most beneficial results, but from my knowledge of the local conditions
I think the county jails are not fit to look after convicts suffering from contagious disease. I think it would be far better, and much more humane to segregate such cases in the penitentiary and treat them there.

I am afraid I do not wholly agree, with those who have spoken on this matter. I would not like to see legislation passed which virtually threw upon the Dominion government the care of incurables by the mere act of the incurable committing a crime. The incurable, in so far as he requires care at all, is the ward of the provincial authorities, and the upon the Dominion government the care of him. Consequently, in endeavouring at least to rid the Dominion of the obligation of accepting a charge which constitutionally is a provincial charge, I am wholly in sympathy with the minister. I only make this comment; in legislating that the man may remain, are you also legislating that the province must keep him? If you are, I am afraid you are doing worse than establishing a wheat board. Can this Parliament legislate to compel the province to maintain a prisoner who has been sentenced to the penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may say that this request has come from the provinces themselves. I do not anticipate any difficulty over it. This has been the practice for years, and there has never been any trouble. In the past, no person suffering from a contagious disease could be admitted to a penitentiary. The prisoner has to be sent somewhere to be treated, and as he comes from the province, if he is suffering from a contagious disease he is sent back to a jail in a district of the province. There is only one question before us, because the question of maintenance does not come in now, and that is the treatment of prisoners suffering from a contagious disease. We could give them their liberty, but they have to be kept somewhere, and the provincial authorities say: Let us take them back to our jails or hospitals, and we will treat them. If any complaint should come from the provincial authorities, we shall consider it and try to ^settle it to the satisfaction of the province. .
What has been the practice in such cases in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The provincial authorities now take the prisoners back to their jails, but there is a doubt whether they have a legal right to do so, and it is
Penitentiary Act

to remove that doubt that we are proposing this amendment.
This amendment does not change the practice at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all.
In the county of Lennox that has always been the practice. If a criminal in the jail is sick, we take care of him in the hospital, and return him to the jail when he is better.

I was surgeon to a county jail in Ontario for about twenty years, and I would point out that no prisoner is sent from a county jail to the penitentiary without the surgeon's certificate that he is free from disease. If he contracts the disease on the road to the penitentiary, the governor of the jail would refuse to take him back. The governor of the jail would not consider that he was entitled to take charge of a man because of his suffering from an infectious disease. Furthermore in the smaller jails in the counties of Ontario absolutely no provision is made for the treatment of diseased patients, and no accommodation ekists for them except in the corridor or in the cell- there is not even a hospital ward in the majority of these institutions. Consequently, if a prisoner suffering from an infectious disease is returned to one of these jails he is put in with the other inmates and thus becomes a menace to their health as well as to the health of those philanthropic people who pay visits to the inmates from time to time. There is 'likewise a lack of hospital accommodation, I think, in connection with the jails in the smaller towns. Under the circumstances I think it will be found that the jail governors will refuse to accept prisoners suffering from infectious disease and will send them back whence they came.

According to the Minister of Justice we are by this legislation only making legal what has been done without authority in the past. Let me say a word or two in reference to the condition of our jails in the province of Nova Scotia. I can supplement what has been said of conditions in the other provinces by stating that I do not know of a jail in my own province even in the city of Halifax, that is equipped to look after a prisoner suffering from infectious disease. There is, on the other hand, a possibility that such legislation as this may make it easier to retain men in the local jails; it has oc-

curred to me that such a thing might be possible by connivance between the local medical officer and the friends of the prisoner. I think I can remember in the practice of my profession the attempt being made to retain a man in a local jail in order not to have the stigma put upon him of having been an inmate of a penitentiary. It does seem to me also, as has been suggested by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) that there is some danger of perpetrating an injustice upon the local authorities. Because, in Nova Scotia, the cost of maintaining a prisoner in jail devolves upon the municipal authorities, in the county of Cumberland, for example, that cost is borne by the county council and not by the provincial authorities. There may be very good reasons for the municipalities objecting to paying for the maintenance of prisoners who have been sentenced to the penitentiary; but there is one thing that we should do as far as we possibly can, and that is to provide humane treatment for the poor devil who has been jailed whilst suffering from an infectious disease. Cases have come under my personal observation of men who have been forced to lie in a pretty close cell, destitute of even sanitary arrangements, suffering and almost dying from infectious disease, and nobody seemed to worry very much about them. I think it would be better practice, wherever possible, to get a man who has been sentenced to the penitentiary sent to that institution as quickly as possible because proper hospital accommodation is obtainable and the needed facilities to look after his particular case.

It is not the province upon whom the financial responsibility tests, and that is a fact I would like to bring to the attention of the minister. I can quite understand the provinces being satisfied with this as legalizing a practice heretofore obtaining, but it is the county that bears the entire cost in connection with these jails-even the surgeon is paid by the county. Now what does this legislation mean? It simply means that it is left to the local municipality to take care of any expense that may be occasioned by the present amendment. They have not the necessary facilities to care for those suffering from infectious disease, and it is not at all likely that those facilities will be provided. It seems to me that if this amendment is to be adopted the rights of the municipalities should be safeguarded by some scheme properly worked out. If

Supply-Insurance
the provinces would undertake this responsibility all well and good; but if they will not do so it simply means that these patients will not get the requisite treatment. It seems to me that when a man receives a sentence which takes him to the penitentiary he becomes a charge upon the federal authorities and it is for them to see that proper care is taken of him. Whether they should go to the extent of providing facilities for treating such patients locally is a doubtful point; but I can assure the minister that legalizing a practice which has prevailed in the past will not do away with the trouble. After all it is most important to see that proper treatment should be provided for these men. That cannot and will not be provided in the local jails, the expense of whose maintenance is now entirely borne by the counties.

In the province of Ontario the Public Health Act prohibits the transfer from one municipality to another of any person suffering from infectious disease. Therefore a prisoner suffering in this way could not be transferred from the penitentiary to a local jail or otherwise without violating the Public Health Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are not proposing by this legislation to change what has been the practice in the past; all that is being done is to legalize the 5 p.m. existing procedure. As to the question of expenditure the obligations of the provinces are not being increased ; they will in the future be the same in this respect as they have been in the past. One hon. member stated that the expense in these cases is paid by the counties. In our province that cost is borne by the provincial authorities. If parliament decides that we should take charge of the prisoners from the day they are convicted, whether they are suffering from infectious disease or not, that is another matter. We are only asking here that the mode of procedure under which the provincial authorities have acted in the past shall be legalized. I cannot say what the experience has been in other provinces but I am not aware that a single complaint has ever been made on this account in the province of Quebec, i Another objection raised is that if the law is amended in the manner proposed, a prisoner may be detained in a provincial jail for the whole term of his sentence, which might be for four or five years. But it should be remembered that the time spent by a prisoner in a provincial jail or a provincial hospital will be counted on his sentence; and should there be any doubt on that score the Minister of. Justice would certainly liberate the prisoner upon the expiration of his term. Therefore, considering all the objections and all the observations which have been made in regard to these two amendments which I have the honour to propose,
I do not see that we can do more to-day than what is proposed in them. We say that we go according to the old rules; we refuse to receive, in penitentiaries, prisoners if they suffer from infectious or contagious diseases, and we authorize the provinces to keep such prisoners in their charge, to treat them and, if possible, to cure them.
I have reason to believe that the explanations I have given are sufficient to convince hon. members of the necessity of these amendments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a small increase in the salary item. That we must expect as there is a constant increase in the insurance business. The number of officials is one less; but, against that, there is an increase in the contingency appropriation, out of which temporary employees will be paid. The increase in the volume of insurance which has to be handled by the department, is very great. Let me give these figures for the purposes of illustration. In 1915, the total fire insurance in force was $3,531,620,802. In 1920, according to the latest figures with which I have been furnished, it amounted to $5,969,872,278. The percentage of increase between 1915 and 1920 in the total fire insurance in force is 69. Between those two years there is an increase of 91 per cent in the net fire insurance premiums received, an increase of 103 per cent in the total life insurance business in force and an increase of 185 per cent in the amount of new life insurance issued. Altogether, these figures indicate, as they must, that there will always be a growing business in that department and this growing business will call, from time to time, for some increases. The additional
Supply-Insurance

amount asked by the superintendent is not large, and I am quite sure it will be only in harmony with the growth of the business.

I observe, of course, what the minister himself has remarked, namely, that efforts at economy in this case have again resulted in an increased expenditure of about eight or nine per cent. I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance particularly acknowledge that, with increase in the functions of government, in the business of government, there necessarily will be some increase in the cost of operation, and, in a word, that if that goes on, as it has been going on, the cause of economy must be confined pretty much to propaganda.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is rather too early to expect any government to indulge in economy in regard to Civil Service departments before there is any opportunity of making any inquiry. As regards my department, I make no boast of economy. I have not dismissed anybody; I took the estimates as I found them last year and I made a few changes. As time rolls on, I hope we can manifest economy in these branches. For the present, I suppose most of the ministers will be obliged to accept, in large degree the estimates of the past year, and time must be allowed for any economy to be exercised. At any rate as regards any branches with which I am connected, I am making no boast of economy at the present time. What will be done in the future remains to be seen.

That remark applies with some force to oases like those of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King), possibly the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) and, perhaps, some others; but if there is one case to which it does not apply, it is that of the Minister of Finance himself. He was Minister of Finance of this country for fifteen years, in the very department in which he is now. He knows the organization of the department. Even in the ten years during which he was out of office, he followed its work and development very closely. I do not doubt at all that he knows intimately most of the higher officials of the department. They are the same people who were there in his time. This is something that he has at his fingers' ends. The Minister of Finance is all too modest when he seeks to convince me that three months would not be ample time for him to see if there was any extravagance in his department

in the matter of civil government. Three months! Why, in three weeks, the Minister of Finance would have a pretty good idea; but with all his experience and knowledge of the department, with all his concentration on that department, for that has been the work of his life, he is now compelled to come to this Parliament and, in every instance so far, not to confess his total inability to ask for any reduction, but rather to ask for something more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If, in the last three months, I had nothing to do but study the Civil Service, in all probability my right hon. friend's remarks would be to the point; but, if he does not know this fact, I have had a great deal to do during the past three months. There are a number of vacancies in my department; my predecessor left some, and they have not been filled yet for the reason that I have not had time to investigate the matter. I have as much desire for economy in my department as I commend to my brother ministers, but time must be allowed for the exercise of economy; it cannot be accomplished in a day.

I trust that is not an intimation that all the vacancies in this department are to be filled. The appropriation put through amounts to about $413,000, and my recollection is that what it costs to run the department is $350,000. I recognize that my hon. friend will have before him circumstances which may require the extra vote. For instance, supposing that he puts into effect, what I think would be a very proper reform, the centralizing of all the bookkeeping of the country in the Finance Department, he may want more money; but I hope, simply because there are vacancies, my hon. friend is not going to fill them at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend left some vacancies, and I may say that I intend to have some of them filled. They will have to be filled by the Civil Service Commission. I do not want to call in question the wisdom of the Civil Service Commission, but I am not sure, under the machinery we have in the Civil Service Commission, we shall get the best men. Some of these vacancies will certainly be filled, and I do not hesitate to say that the men of my department are overworked. We are, however dealing at present with the Insurance Department. I think in that respect there is no ground for criticism.

I have never disputed the desire of the minister to reduce, and

Is the current report true, that the Auditor General is retiring?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He has intimated his desire to retire and it is expected that leave of absence will be granted him up to the first of October, at which time it is contemplated he will retire. He has been for no less a period than fifty years in the public service.

In connection with the
estimates of several departments, members
have repeatedly inquired upon whose recommendation the civil servants are appointed, and it was stated in reply a few nights ago that they were employed on the recommendation of the deputies or other officers higher up in the service. I think that is a most arbitrary proceeding. Members of Parliament, who are responsible for moneys voted in this House, desire to do everything possible to promote the efficiency of the public service. But we are led to believe, in certain instances, that departments are overmanned and officers higher up overpaid, as evidenced^ in the frequent increases asked for in civil government estimates. In view of this fact I have wondered whether it would not be advisable to appoint a parliamentary committee at this session to look into the various departments, with the deputy ministers and other officers of the Government, to ascertain and report to Parliament in what directions possible retrenchment, without impairment to the efficiency of the service, might be effected. I think there is good work in that connection that a special committee of the House could undertake, and I am sure that deputy ministers would co-operate with such a committee. I offer this merely as a suggestion.

Although
there is a blanketing of officials in this item, there seems to be a considerable amount carried in the contingency vote, as well, for clerical and other assistance. It is suggested that certain temporary employees will be put on the permanent staff. I hope the minister will not transfer them all to the permanent staff, because the permanent staff is ample as it is. I had hoped that the department might be brought up to something like a state of modern efficiency, so that the requirements of modern business might be met, providing a proper audit that would adequately safeguard the Treasury, especially in regard to petty cash items. If that is to be done the department will have to be largely reconstituted. Otherwise my hon. friend will find that the character of the work will not conduce to a proper up-to-date system such as I suggest. I hope, I repeat, that he does not intend to place all the temporaries on the permanent staff, because we have enough permanent employees as it is. But if he does so, surely he will not need the vote for clerical assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know how the word "blanketing," as it is used fre-

quently in connection with the Estimates, originated. If it means the transfer of temporary employees to the permanent list, it will be found that during the past year a good deal of that sort of transfer was made. I cannot say that the present Government has done nothing of that kind, but I do know that efforts have been made in the various departments to transfer many of the officials from the temporary to the permanent list and the matter has been held for further consideration. I agree that when you transfer a man from the temporary to the permanent list he acquires a larger vested right and it is harder to displace him.
