speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, a going concern like these farms cannot be administered with any degree of success without a corresponding increase in expenditure. I am sure my hon. friend from Victoria City (Mr. Toimie) has frequently noticed in the past that opportunities of spending a little more money on these experimental farms have increased, but during the war the vote was held down, and properly so I think. Since then conditions have not improved very much, from a financial standpoint, and in fact the vote is still being held down.
I think there was a continual increase during the war.

And there will be now; but notwithstanding that there may be an increase in some items, the expenditure generally is being held down. There are twenty-two experimental farms located throughout the Dominion, and certain extensions are made from time to time of the work they are engaged in. As we go over the vote I shall be able to explain in detail how the aggregate is made up. A new farm was established last year at Swift Current that my hon. friend is familiar with. It is in a very primitive condition yet, and a reasonable amount of expenditure.has to be incurred in order to get it properly launched. The vote does not contemplate the addition of any new experimental farms this year. An item will be found later of possible expenditure for the acquisition of necessary land in the event of one or two more farms being established, but that would be as far as we would go this year.

This is a very large amount of money and we are not supplied with any details. I am interested, as one of these experimental farms is situated in my constituency, and I know its work has been curtailed very much, in fact too much it is claimed. Will the minister give us details of this vote?

We have a mass of information here, Mr. Chairman, but it would not be convenient to burden the committee with the whole of it. If my hon. friend will particularize what he wishes to be informed about I shall be glad to help him. We have all the farms tabulated here.
Beginning in the east, we have farms at the following points: Charlottetown, P.E.I., Kentville, N.S., Nappan, N.S., Fredericton, N.B., St. Anne de la Pocatiere, Que., Cap Rouge, Que., Lennoxville, Que., La Ferme, Que., Kapuskasing, Ont., Morden, Man., Brandon, Man., Indian Head, Sask., Rosthern, Sask., Scott, Sask., Swift Current, Sask., Lacombe, Alta., Lethbridge, Alta., Agassiz, B.C., Invermere, B.C., Sydney, B.C., and Summerland, B.C. There are also a certain number of sub-stations.
How much was spent on the Fredericton farm last year, and how much is proposed to be spent this year? Is the vacant position of superintendent of that farm to be filled right away?

The total amount spent last year was $40,482. The position of superintendent has been vacant for some time and is in the process of being filled. The position will have to be advertised by the Civil Service Commission, and that usually takes a couple of weeks. When the applications are all in, there will be the usual procedure of appointing a board to examine the applicants.
How much is to be spent this year?
$42,882, an increase of nearly $3,000.

The work of that farm has been very largely curtailed; it does not appear that there will be any extension of activities in the coming year. I wish also to point out that in order to encourage good men to remain in the service, the principle of promotion should be adopted. The superintendent of the, farm resigned last year, and the work has since been carried on by a man born on a good New Brunswick farm. He had the advantage of living on that farm for a considerable length of time, and subsequently had the advantage of experience in a banking institution. He has been acting as assistant superintendent for the past three years. I hope that his claims to promotion will be given serious consideration. The department can exercise considerable influence in the appointment of a new superintendent, and I trust that the principle of promotion will commend itself to the minister and his officials as applying to this case. It will not be a popular move if some one who is not now in the service is appointed to that position, and if what I have heard is true, it is the intention to bring in an outsider.

The principle
enunciated by my hon friend is quite sound. I do not know the gentleman to whom he refers; I understand his name is Taylor.

The principle is sound, and should be followed wherever possible. I would not like to say just how much influence we have in the matter of the appointment. The suggestion has been made that the amount of this vote seems rather large, but considering the importance of agriculture I do not think it is at all excessive. In tact, I think it could be largely increased with a great amount of profit to the agrarian interests of Canada. The minister, speaking of the farm at Swift Curent, said that it was in a very primitive state. Did I understand him to say that a sum would be included in the Supplementary Estimates to provide this farm with buildings, or is the amount for that purpose included in the general vote for experimental farms?

Certain minor
buildings will be taken care of by this vote. It is quite probable that when the Supplementary Estimates come down they will contain a further sum for buildings That, of course, will depend on the condition of the finances of the country.

Will the minister give me the same information in respect to the Swift Current farm that he gave the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), in respect to the amount spent last year and the appropriation for this year?

The minister says that money will be voted to provide new build-

ings that are urgently needed to meet the conditions of agriculture in the West. Agriculture is a line of work which should not suffer through lack of this equipment, and we should not hesitate to vote the money necessary for that purpose. There are other parts of the country where money could profitably be spent on buildings of this kind, and I reserve the privilege of speaking on this subject on the first opportunity when other estimates are presented.

With regard to the inquiry of my hon. friend (Mr. Lewis), I may say that there is an item of $75,000 in the Public Works estimates for repairs and extensions which would take care of certain necessary building at these various experimental farms. As I have said, the matter of going on with new buildings of any considerable size is still under consideration, and if any provision under that head is to be made, it will have to be included in an additional vote to be brought down later.

The minister said that
$40,000 odd would be expended on the farm to which reference was made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). Would he give me similar information in respect to Swift Current?

The amount
spent last year was $19,450. This year is is $25,450.

Is any appropriation included in this item to open up an experimental farm in northern British Columbia? We have a large area up there which is rich in an agricultural sense, lying in the neighbourhood of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. The conditions there are different from those existing in any other part of British Columbia, and different from those on the prairie. It is a country that will be very valuable in the future as a live stock country, and more particularly as a dairy country. It is very productive in the way of hay, roots, and such things as are necessary for the proper carrying on of dairying. The area up there is immense. It is a country that at the present time is perhaps a little subject to frost, but it is one where an experimental farm would render very valuable service, indeed, if established in the near future, to the settlers in that part of British Columbia. I would be glad to know if there is an

Supply-Experimental Farms
appropriation included in this item for that purpose.

That is one place I had in mind when I spoke of experimental farms. There is an appropriation of $30,000, but just where it will be expended I cannot say. It will take some time to select the locality. I am in hopes that next summer I shall be able to visit that country. The locality we had in mind for an experimental farm out there is on the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific between the main range of mountains and the coast mountains. That is a splendid territory capable of a great deal of development in a colonization way. Of course, we cannot expect new settlers with very little resources to do much demonstration work and make a living. So far as my information goes, that will be the next district to have an experimental farm, but before making any decision I would like to visit that country, not only for that purpose, but for many other reasons. I had the pleasure of discussing this matter with a number of members from British Columbia, and they seemed to think that an experimental farm somewhere between the main range and the coast mountains is the proper place; but just where I am not prepared to say at the present time.
How many experimental farms are there in British Columbia at the present time, how many substations, and how many demonstration farms?

There are four experimental farms, one sub-station, and I believe twelve illustration stations. I will give my hon. friend a list of them later. These illustration farms are small allotments running from twenty-five to forty acres, frequently leased from a local farmer. At all events, that is the usual practice on the prairie.

I should also like the number of substations and illustration farms in each of the provinces, with their area, also the amount expended in connection with each of them, particularly the expenditure, outside of the civil government vote, for the permanent farm labour on each farm, the wages of the foremen, superintendents, and so forth.

May I ask if the
minister expects to get a successor for Professor Saunders, who carried on insect pest research work in the maritime provinces, also what is being done with regard
to devising ways and means of overcoming potato disease, finding out the cause and the best preventive measures.

I can now give my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) a list of the illustration stations in British Columbia: Armstrong, Bar-riere, Comox, Frances Lake, Kamloops, Ker-vilie, Prince George, Smithers, Salmon Arm, Telkwa and Vanderhoof.
I would also like to know the revenue derived from the farms in each of the provinces.

I presume my
hon. friend means the gross revenue. There is not very much net revenue.
Are the expenses of the illustration farms included in this item? Is it the policy of the Government to establish more illustration farms in Canada?

In reply to the first question, yes. With regard to the establishment of more illustration farms, in the natural development of an institution of this kind there will, of course, be more farms. There are not very many in the different provinces, partly due to the fact that some of the provincial governments, the Ontario government, for instance, have taken up this kind of work, in a measure, and partly because there has not been a great demand for it, and such demand as there was, was being gratified. I remember that in the western provinces this work was being taken up in a small way before the Dominion government went into it. It is not an easy matter to get a suitable location and a suitable farmer to take charge of one of these illustration farms. The work is not overpaid, and it requires a lot of time and care, and a man with an experimental turn of mind, but in the majority^ of cases we are fairly successful. Occasionally we get a man who does not come up to our expectations, and in that case we eliminate him and get another man. There is no capital outlay in connection with these farms, except in one or two instances in the Peace river country, where a certain amount of capital has been expended. As a rule the land is just leased, the farms ranging from twenty-five to forty acres. We do not undertake much risk in these matters but occasionally our anticipations may not altogether be realized. Even so, I think the work can be extended with advantage.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock, Item No. 41, page 22 of the Estimates, was under consideration. Shall the resolution carry?

Before we rose at six o'clock the minister was making some rather pertinent remarks regarding the value of ex-peTimental farms in new districts, and he seemed to be questioning the value of those in the old districts. I would call his attention to the situation in his own province with which he is very well acquainted. At Indian Head there is a farm which has been in operation for some years, I do not know just how many. By the Auditor General's Report for 1920 I see that that farm cost $44,482 that year, while the inincome from it was only $2,955.66. We have at Saskatoon, as the minister well knows, a large farm operated in connection with the university, at which all kinds of experiments can be conducted; forty-two miles distant is the experimental farm at Ros-thern, and1 about one hundred miles west of it is another at Scott. Now, realizing the importance of economy at this particular time, I am wondering whether there is not a certain amount of duplication there- whether all that experimental work could not be better carried on at Saskatoon and the money thus Saved employed usefully in some other direction. I am also wondering whether these- farms as they become better established cannot toe made selfsustaining. When one looks at the immense amount of money spent on them, and the small returns received from the sale of produce, the contrast is striking.

This is a very interesting and important question. I think every member of the committee will recognize that no matter where the experimental farm may be located, there will surely be some local benefit accrue from it. When we rose at six o'clock I was discussing the relative values of experimental farms in old and new districts. I believe that in the new districts we will probably get three or four times as much value in proportion to our expenditure as we get in the older districts. That will hold good whether it is an old farm in a new district like Indian Head, or a new farm in
an old district in Ontario. But inasmuch as the old farms were established at Brandon and Indian Head when these were new districts, naturally we are rather disposed to continue them.	[DOT]
With regard to the farms at Scott and Rosthern I think the latter was located before the university was established at Saskatoon, if I remember rightly.
I think so.

That accounts
for its proximity of only forty miles. The farm at Scott is in a peculiar district in regard to soil, which is of an entirely different character to that around Saskatoon, and therefore I suppose the distance of only one hundred miles was not considered an objection to its location at that point. But quite apart from that, I cannot help thinking that since the University of Saskatchewan has been established at Saskatoon as a state university, that is, combining in its curriculum agriculture as well as the arts and sciences, the whole question of duplication might be considered. We have not yet had sufficient time to deal with it conclusively. But for the sake of standing by what is generally [DOT]looked upon as a good thing, I do not think we should countenance duplication such as my hon. friend refers to. I have discussed this matter with Dean Rutherford of the Agricultural College on more than one occasion, having in view the possibility of some time merging those farms into the activities of the university. That can only be accomplished by the joint action of the province and the Dominion, but it is worth considering. As a good many of us know, the university authorities look forward to establishing a number of stations throughout Saskatchewan tributary to the university, and it occurs to me that some of these farms that we look upon as instances of duplication might be made part of the university's activities. Possibly the work might be entered into jointly by the Dominion and the province, we still retaining supervision over the work for a time, at all events.
There is no doubt that with respect to the older established farms we feel sometimes that we do not get full value for what they cost us. But it must be remembered that the value of the Indian Head farm when the old territories of Alberta and Saskatchewan were one was simply incalculable.

Agreed.

But that was
thirty years ago. Despite present conditions, I feel almost like continuing that farm even though it may have passed the point of maximum usefulness for the sake of the work it has done in years gone by. But apart from sentimental reasons, there is no doubt the day will come when these older farms will be required for other purposes, such as stock breeding and' multiplying certain new varieties of grains developed at the experimental farm here. For those purposes they are still useful, but a large proportion of their usefulness for the purposes for which they were originally designed has automatically passed away. That is unavoidable, and cannot be regarded as in any sense derogatory to the general plan of experimental farms.
But the point I wish to bring out is that during the first twenty-five years an experimental farm in a country like that is at its period of maximum usefulness to the community: that maximum, however, gradually declines as we pass into a new era, until finally the time arrives when we have to consider the question of soil fertility and cognate matters.

I agree thoroughly with what the hon. minister has said with regard to the usefulness of these farms for the first twenty-five years, and as to their further usefulness afterwards as to stock breeding and seed multiplying areas. The only point I had in mind was not the cutting down of the estimates, but of seeing that we get as full value as we possibly can for the money spent. I know that he is so thoroughly familiar with his province that it is only necessary to draw his attention to the matter for him to do his very best to that end.

The minister mentioned the differences between the soil at Scott and at Saskatoon. There is a vast portion of the province of Saskatchewan lying north of those points that has no experimental farm, and the difference in soil is far greater. I refer to the country lying north of probably townships 43 and 44. This is generally known as park country, and is devoted principally to stock-raising and dairying, besides raising grain fairly extensively. I hope the minister will keep this in mind so that if there is any change in the arrangements that portion of the West will be selected in which to conduct experiments. There is ample opportunity for

establishing experimental stations in that northern country.

I gather from the information given by the minister that there are twenty-two or twenty-three experimental farms in the Dominion. How many of these are located in each province? And what is the basis for apportioning so many farms to each province?

I do not think
there is any recognized basis. In the older districts they had to do without experimental farms in the earlier days. For instance, if one hundred years ago a philanthropist had offered to give assistance in this respect-for there was no government money for the purpose in those days -there would have been many opportunities for the establishment of experimental farms in the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec. But to-day the tendency-and I think it is a correct one-is to establish these farms where they will do the most good, to assist the new settler in demonstrating the capabilities of the particular area in which he has cast his lot rather than oblige him to do the demonstrating himself and at the same time try to make a living. In such cases the government comes to the rescue. Such is the farm at Indian Head, referred to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales). Such is the one we have in view along the line of the Transcontinental in British Columbia, about which the hon. gentleman for Victoria city (Mr. Tolmie) spoke. The requirements of. some of the provinces are not so great in this respect; they are settled and established; their people have for the last hundred years been demonstrating the possibilities and capabilities of those areas. I do not think it would be wise to establish an arbitrary basis, relating to population, geographical division, or otherwise, upon which the opening up of experimental farms should be carried on.

I judge from the
remarks of the minister that there is no particular basis upon which these farms are established; I presume the district that brings the greatest pressure to bear upon him gets the farm. I remind the minister, then, that our district is new, and assure him that we are going to bring a lot of pressure to bear upon him in the near future.

I have particular sympathy for my hon. friend, because I

Supply-Experimental Farms
have had very pleasant relations with that territory.

I have always
felt that legislation originating in this Parliament is of a federal nature, and that dre should look at things from the point of view of the general welfare of the whole country, not from the narrow or provincial point of view. But I am inclined to think that instead of broadening out, instead of having an outlook more national in its character, we are really becoming more provincial than we were a few years ago. I am sorry to have to admit it, but that seems to be the case. I believe there has been a disposition on the part of the older provinces to meet the requirements of the newer districts so far as that can reasonably be done. It is a somewhat significant thing that of late years there has been a tendency to make it appear that the agricultural industry has been receiving great consideration at the hands of the government. I am not now referring to any particular government; this has been the case with all governments. There has been a tendency to vote large sums of money for agricultural purposes, sometimes with no proper conception of what real value shall be obtained for the expenditure made. In some instances where large grants have been given we have not received, I am inclined to think, the value that we should Furthermore, the provinces are not as careful in the expenditure of. grants made to them by the federal government as they would be of moneys raised by themselves. I am satisfied that in our own province- and I am referring now not only to experimental farms, but to other things for which we have been voting money-there is a tendency to say: Well, this money comes very easily; we will let it go very easily.
I hope no one will think that I underestimate the value of experimental farms. In fact, I attach much more importance to them and to their value than the Minister of Agriculture does, judging from his remark that after a farm has been established for twenty-five years, seventy-five per cent of its value disappears. On the contrary, my view is that the older the province or district becomes and the more the science of agriculture develops from year to year, the greater is the need for experimental work. I am not sure that some of the difficulties which are being experienced in some of the newer districts could not be overcome if we had better system of experimental farms, and the work was
brought home to the people a little more closely than it now is. While the land is new, rich and fertile, it is an easy matter to settle on it and carry on what is called farming, but a great deal of which is not farming at all but exploitation of the fertility which has been stored up in the soil for centuries.
So far as Ontario is concerned, we have never taken exception to any grants that have been made for experimental farms in the newer districts. But I hold in my hand a pamphlet issued and circulated all over Canada by the Dominion Experimental Farm, on the face of which is a map indicating the location of the various farms, throughout Canada. It is somewhat significant that from the Central Experimental Farm, located at Ottawa, in the extreme eastern part of the province, you can go west for five hundred miles into what is a fairly good agricultural district in Ontario and you will not find another experimental farm, with the exception of a small experimental station for tobacco growing in the county of Kent. Moreover, there are three, four, or five farms in each of the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba. When you come to Ontario there is practically a blank; when you come to Quebec, you will find that it is dotted with farms, and so on down through the maritime provinces.
Now, this thing has surely reached the stage where we shall have to register some objection to what has been going on. It is true that in 1916 a farm was established in the bush in northern Ontario, and I believe it is doing good work,-I was a strong advocate of having something done there. But that does not remedy the difficulty. The old settled districts of Ontario have been forced to establish farms themselves, and between those farms and the Dominion system of experimental farms there is no connection. We were passing estimates last night to encourage immigration: you will find that the first thing a prospective immigrant wants to know is what are the possibilities of the various provinces, and he will naturally look at the report of the experimental farms as found in these circulars and in other literature sent out by the Experimental Farms branch. An injustice is done to Ontario, or to any other province, when it does not figure prominently in these publications.
The statement has frequently been made that the Central Experimental Farm near



Supply-Experimental Farms
the city of Ottawa serves the whole province of Ontario, and that the money expended in connection with that farm is money expended on the province of Ontario. I think any one who understands the situation will agree that the Central farm has been located near this city for the benefit of the whole Dominion, and that many of the officials connected with it are carrying on their work in the different provinces. The Central farm consists of 467 acres and was established in 1886. There is one feature about the Central farm to which I am going to call the attention of the committee, and I am not bringing this matter up to-night simply because we have a new government and a new minister, because I have done the same thing when conditions were different. I have pointed out before that there is an absolute waste of money in connection with our experimental farm system, and that we do not get that efficient supervision and management to which we are entitled. On looking over the public accounts for the present year I was somewhat surprised to find that notwithstanding the deflation which has taken place in practically every other branch of the service, there was expended on the Central farm near Ottawa during the past year for ordinary farm labour no less a sum than $179,387.18. That is an increase of about $40,000. I do not know whether the increase in the estimates before us is to meet the deficit the minister expects next year. It is true that he gave what practically amounted to a promise to establish a new farm in British Columbia if conditions warranted it, but an increase of $40,000 for farm labour on this little farm close to the city of Ottawa is surely something that requires an explanation under present conditions. An experimental farm in order to render service must show that it is able to practise the methods it is endeavouring to teach. Otherwise, if it merely exists for conducting experiments, it need not be conducted on so large a scale. This increase in the cost of farm labour at the Central farm will seem strange to many who have not inquired into this matter, but I have seen this increase going on year after year. I have paid close attention to what is going on, and I am satisfied that the Central farm near Ottawa is more of a show place for visitors from all over the Dominion than it is an experimental farm. It is all very well to grow tomatoes and oranges in January and February under glass, but is that rendering any good service to the people of this community?

Is that the sort of experiments we want? The province of Ontario is establishing a new farm in the county of Kent, with a view to developing the possibilities in that part of the province. We have also a fruit farm at Vinelands in the Niagara district. The returns show that the province of Ontario grows practically all the tender fruits, and yet the province itself has to establish and maintain these farms. The Dominion government has absolutely refused to give any assistance. There is another farm at Kemptville, which was established and is maintained by the provincial government. Then there is the experimental farm in connection with the agricultural college at Guelph, which is also maintained by the province. This province pays nearly one-half of the customs revenue of the country, about 48 per cent, and yet it is compelled to establish and maintain its own experimental farms. We get practically no consideration from the Government in this matter.
The minister states that an experimental farm cannot do the good in an old settled district that it can in a new country. That may be, but I believe there are about twenty-five illustration farms in the province of Quebec, and not one in the province of Ontario. An illustration station or something of that kind might be all that would be required in a new district, where you have not the facilities for carrying on scientific work. I pointed out a year ago when the estimates of this department were up for consideration that the factory output of dairy products in one small county of Ontario was greater than the output of the1 provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and British Columbia combined. This goes to show what can be done by intensive farming, and it is something that an experimental farm should bring home to the people. The experimental farms should blaze the way and show the people of this country that they can practise what they preach; they should lead, and not simply follow. Otherwise, the money expended is very largely wasted.
The minister pointed out in his opening remarks that a farm was going to be established in the province of British Columbia. I believe there was some idea last year, and it may still be under consideration, of establishing a flax experimental station somewhere in western Ontario. I am not sure whether the purchase of a site has been made. It is true that during the war flax growing increased very consider-

Supply-Experimental Farms
ably in Ontario. In one part of western Ontario people went into it on quite a large scale, and many of them were practically ruined as a result. As long ago as I can rememlber there have been numerous flax mills in western Ontario, and looking over the territory where they were located forty years ago you can see the effects of flax growing in that district up to this day. In the months of June and1 July those lands are as yellow as can be with wild mustard which was introduced and went to seed on these land's, and it has been impossible to eradicate it. You could not induce any one in that district who had experience in the growing of flax in the early days to engage in that industry to-day. There may be a considerable amount of flax being grown in western Ontario to-day, but that is only a temporary condition, because we Cannot compete with the cheap labour of such countries as India, Belgium and Russia, where they have grown flax successfully for years. I know there are experiments being conducted at the Experimental Farm along that line, and during the time flax growing was a profitable industry no doubt such experiments served a useful purpose. That is the great value of an experimental farm.
But I want to emphasize the fact that the newer districts are not so much in need of experimental work as the old districts are. It is in the latter that scientific methods must be applied, and we must adopt different methods from those we have followed in the past even in the old districts, if we are going to successfully compete with other agricultural countries where labour and land are much cheaper. All you have to do to realize that fact is to look at the imports into Canada. Then you will find that even with conditions as they are at the present time, staple commodities such as we can grow without any difficulty in this country are being imported and sold in our own markets notwithstanding the fact that we have very substantial duties upon such importations. Imagine, if you can, the conditions such as we have had during the year, ending on 31st March last, when over two million pounds of butter were brought into Canada from Great Britain under the British preference and sold to our people. Let me remind my hon. friends to my left that exporters from Great Britain can send commodities into Canada at a cheaper rate than they can be imported from United States. Millions of pounds are being imported into the
51i
Dominion under the conditions as they now exist. Look at the imports of bacon and beef, and other food products that are entering the country. Look at the quantity of eggs which is now being imported into Canada under the conditions I have described. We must adopt different methods if we are going to compete with other countries; although I understand the policy of hon. members opposite, and of hon. members to my left, to be to put all foodstuffs on the free list. The Lord only knows what will happen to the Canadian farmer when that day comes, because under the present conditions it is utterly impossible for the farmer in the old districts to compete with the outside world in production of their foodstuffs.
I ask the minister to say to-night whether he can-with all the money that has been spent, amounting to a million and a quarter or a half of dollars-state the actual cost of production of one of the articles I have mentioned at the farm? He is unable to do so, he makes no attempt to comply with the request. Individual farmers are conducting experiments along this line and are able to do so; but if you wait for information from the experimental farm on that question you will wait a long time.
Now, these are some of the things that I think might well engage the attention of the Government and Parliament on this occasion. I say we are not getting value for the money we are expending in this direction; and it is not fair to those who are engaged in agriculture to point to the millions of dollars that are being spent for supposedly agricultural purposes and then say, " How well you are being taken care of." Before the House rose at six o'clock I asked some questions with regard to the number of experimental farms in each province with a view to ascertaining the cost of carrying on these farms and the revenue derived therefrom. I think the minister and those associated with him in the department should be able to place before the committee some of the actual benefits that have resulted from the experiments carried on at these farms. They should be able to show what the actual cost of production is, and whether such methods of farming could be carried on at a profit or not. To my mind that is one of the important things that an experimental farm should be able to demonstrate. I would ask the minister therefore whether he is able to give the com-

mittee the information asked for in regard to these matters.

My deputy has
the information here but it is not classified in exactly the way in which my hon. friend wants it. While he is compiling it in the desired form I might answer my hon. friend in respect to two or three other matters. My hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has almost convinced me that the province of Ontario is very much slighted in the matter of the distribution of experimental farms. If with all this new information he has placed at my disposal I can equalize these matters somewhat I am sure I shall be delighted to do so. I am informed that one experimental farm has been established of recent years at Kapuskasing. My predecessor in office, very wisely, I think, on the advice of his deputy and the Director of Experimental Farms located that farm in what is known as New Ontario along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. If any error was committed in this respect Mr. Burrell was at fault but I do not think he did err; it was a logical thing to do. There may come a time when we will have sufficient revenues to establish these institutions in the old as well as the new districts; but so long as our means are limited surely the new districts are the proper places in which to establish these farms in order to obtain the maximum results from the money expended. I am told there has been a tobacco station established at Harrow.

Yes, in the county of Essex. I think it is one of the greatest possible compliments to old Ontario that her agriculture is in such a highly developed condition that she does not require any of these experimental farms or demonstration stations. Our forefathers did the demonstrating in old Ontario fifty and one hundred years ago at immense toil and labour. To-day Parliament comes to the assistance of the new districts and undertakes demonstrations which the old pioneers in Ontario had to do for themselves.
My hon. friend seems to be quite positive that we have not been able to demonstrate at the Central Experimental
9 p.m. Farm what it cost to produce various commodities. Even if that were true I do not think we would be subject to any great amount of censure, because you cannot farm on a commercial scale when you are carrying on experiments at experimental farms or demonstra-

tion stations. I do not know that any such institution in the world was ever expected to show as good results as a farm conducted on a commercial scale. Notwithstanding that fact, however, I am informed that many of the Government bulletins and pamphlets do contain figures of the very nature the hon. member desires, showing exactly the cost of producing butter, eggs, meat and many other commodities grown on the farm. Such a thing is not always done by experimental farms because as a rule the showing obtained by them is not as good, measured by dollars and cents, as in the case of commercial farming. That is not the way we measure the value of the experimental farms; but, however, that is too big a subject to enter upon to-night. I merely give the hon. member the information he asks for and I do not make these remarks in any spirit of criticism of my hon. friend. I would say this however: There is a general impression- formed from speeches made sometimes in this House or from careless remarks uttered by gentlemen outside-that these experimental farms are simply huge centres of slothfulness and uselessness, just simply a resort where people can congregate, a sort of haven of refuge, a sort of agricultural senate as it were. That is not the case. Then we have another class of gentlemen -I will not say in the House although I have heard it myself-who never miss an opportunity of slandering the Civil Service of this country, claiming they are enjoying huge salaries, and that they are tumbling over each other and working only one-half the time. Personally I do not believe the greater part of that kind of talk. I have not discovered it at all events. That kind of cheap popularity does not go very far.
Is the hon. gentleman sure about what he says regarding the Senate?

I was just in
need of an illustration at the time, and I could not think of anything else.

I should like to say a word in connection with the establishment of an experimental farm at some point along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I fully agreed with the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) when he said it would greatly contribute to the welfare of the district if an experimental farm

should he established in that part of the country. There is a growing community; in fact, no other community that I know has a brighter prospect than the one along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific if the people there are properly looked after in this matter of agricultural education. Many people are coming in from the prairie provinces and settling; and numbers of our returned men have settled there. An hon. member stated that the growing of flax impoverishes the soil.
I worked in the old country on a farm where flax had been grown for a hundred years; it is being grown there still, and I believe it will be grown there for another hundred years. Flax is one of the best paying crops that they have in the old country, and I do not think the hon. member who made that statement was speaking from practical experience. I think the Minister of Agriculture is using very good judgment in proposing to establish an experimental farm at some point along the Grand Trunk Pacific. Is an experimental farm going to be established at Can ora, Saskatchewan? A few years ago the department purchased a quarter section there for that purpose; but for some reason nothing was done. The people in that district are anxious to know whether an experimental farm is going to be established there.

When the minister is
spreading these farms around, I hope he will not forget Dauphin.

I should like to hold out some hopes to all hon. gentlemen with regard to this matter, and I believe I can. My deputy informs me that the item of $30,000, of which I spoke before six o'clock, as being for the establishment of one farm, is for two farms. One of them is to be established along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific near the coast. If hon. members have any recommendations to make, I would ask them not to do so by correspondence, as I am overwhelmed
now. As they see me in the corridors and elsewhere, I shall be happy to receive representations. I may say that many places have been mentioned as second choice. I think the figures which have just been submitted by the minister substantiate practically every word that I said. I was a little surprised that the minister should make any reference to anyone making remarks with a view to obtaining some cheap popularity. As regards the Civil Service, I made a statement regarding the amount paid for farm labour on the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa, the amount being $179,600, which I considered was altogether out of proportion to the necessities of the Central farm. Before six o'clock, the minister practically told us that there was $30,000 in the Estimates for an experimental farm in British Columbia. He says now that there is apparently a demand from practically every constituency for an experimental farm; that three of them are going to be established, and, consequently, he is going to keep us all guessing, so that we shall all be in good humour and hopeful as long as no more definite information than that is furnished. This is a serious matter, and it is one that it is not very pleasant to refer to. I have criticized sometimes when people thought that I should not criticize; but I believe I have been sincere in every word that I have ever uttered in regard to the injustice that has been done to Ontario. The minister very glibly refers to Ontario, and, according to him, it is a

Supply-Experimental Farms
great compliment to the people of Ontario that they do not require experimental farms. They do require experimental farms; they are establishing them, and they are paying for them. Because the Dominion government will not do that they have to do it themselves. The minister made reference to the farm at Kapuskasing. I referred to the fact that a farm had been established at Kapuskasing down in the bush where an illustration farm would do just as good work as a farm involving a large expenditure of money. But before that farm was established, the province of Ontario established, near the Grand Trunk Pacific, at Monteith, an experimental farm which had been conducted for a number of years before the Dominion government established the one at Kapuskasing. Even with the experimental farm at Kapuskasing, what do we find? We find another one in Quebec a short distance from it. Consequently, these two farms are very close together; but for over BOO miles west from the Central Experimental Farm, you will not find another experimental farm in the chief agricultural district of Ontario. We are not clamouring for the establishment of experimental farms; we have not been urging their establishment upon the Government, because, during the last few years, everyone knows the need for economy. The time has surely come when we must practise economy everywhere, in this House and outside of it, if we are going to overcome the difficulties with which we are confronted. There is no need of. imagining that, by making appeals for assistance in a certain locality or constituency, we are going to get something for that constituency and that we are going to overcome our difficulties in that way. We must assist the Government to the utmost of our power in endeavouring to meet conditions which are very difficult. That is the reason why I am pointing out these things and stating that this extravagance which is being practised on the Central Experimental Farm, must cease, or we cannot expect to see practised in other branches of the Government that economy which should be practised.
It is really worth while studying the Auditor General's Report. We have been paying a bonus to the civil servants, and that bonus has been going to men engaged as labourers on the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa. That method applied throughout. Many of these people were hired for a few months, but a great many were employed by the year, and in addition

to the salary they drew they were given a bonus. I do not know whether that was the case last year, but certainly it was the year before. The experimental farm system in this country has become so lopsided that I think the remarks made by the member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales) might very well be considered. If some provinces have to do all this work, I think the time has arrived when each province should conduct its own experiments. Certainly one province should not be discriminated against and another province shown favour. There should be a more equitable system than the one now in vogue.

While Ontario
really has only two experimental farms, nevertheless in this Central Farm there is more work being done and more money spent than in any other province in the Dominion.
The minister says that there are in New Brunswick one experimental farm and twelve illustration stations. What are the locations of these stations, and where is the experimental farm?
Are there any demonstration farms in any of the provinces?

They are really all demonstration farms. They are usually classified into experimental farms, demonstration farms, and illustration stations. These are all really interchangeable terms, but by usage they have been applied to designate particular kinds of farms.

I have listened with interest to the discussion for several minutes, and I think profitable contributions have been made by the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) and some other members. I sympathise with a good deal of what the minister has said. The experimental farms have done good work in the various provinfces throughout the Dominion, and I agree with the minister to this extent, that there is perhaps more need cf experimental stations in new sections, because settlers going into these places do not know what the land is adapted to grow, and the Government should bear the expense of experimenting on crops in those sections for a time. In Ontario we need a demonstration farm. My idea of such a farm is one conducted under the supervision of government officials on a purely self-paying basis, so that the actual expense to the Government would be very little if any. I have thought for some

Supply-Experimental Farms
time that the ideal experimental farm could be conducted in such a way that all that would be required to prove whether or not it was successfully managed would be the expense of a book-keeper. Such a farm should have the services of a graduate of one of the Ontario agricultural colleges. Let him turn his college education to practical account in the locality in which he is stationed, and demonstrate to the people that farming can be carried on successfully. He could eliminate a good deal of the cost which we have in connection with the experimental farms to-day. We should encourage, through our agricultural colleges and experimental farms, the proper use of a system of book-keeping. Every successful farmer should keep a system of books and from time to time, or annually, examine them to see whether there has been a profit or a loss for the twelve months. In other words, the farm should be managed, so far as its accounts are concerned, just as an ordinary business is conducted.
I do not see why this cannot be done in the older parts of the provinces, at any rate, in connection with the government experimental farms. The expense entailed by this system would be trifling to the Government, while the educational value to the people would be very considerable indeed. I submit that this is something we need very much, and this is what I mean by a demonstration farm.

I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Pritchard) and I have been thinking about the same thing for half an hour. As a matter of fact, I had, written on a sheet of paper, a suggestion which I will now offer to the minister, that in addition to the $30,000 for the new provinces that need experimental farms, he could save $30,730 on Rosthern and $26,256 on Scott, by placing these farms on a commercial basis. They are well located, their lands are good, and they have good buildings; and I would charge them a moderate interest, say 5 per cent, and let them pay their way and prove that farming can be made a commercial success. Since coming to Ottawa and attending the meetings of the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization, I have found that a good many of our friends think that we are pulling a sort of poor mouth and stretching our tale of woe a little too much. They cannot believe that conditions are as we say. Well, here is a chance for the Government themselves actually to prove where the fault lies and whether the farmer is really a poor business man who does not work long enough hours. I find in the Public Accounts that the
farm at Rosthern pays $14,443 for labourers' wages, in addition to a superintendent and assistant superintendent at a total of nearly $6,000 more, while Scott pays $17,500 for labour and overseeing. I know men who work farms of the same size from which they do not receive a total income in any way approaching these amounts spent in wages. I am sure the minister and his department would perform a really useful service if they would put two or three of these farms on a real commercial basis for a few years.

The other night I asked the minister a question with regard to the record of performance in the poultry industry and he informed me that the matter would be taken up to-night. Previous ministers in the late government put into effect a record of performance of a practical nature along the lines suggested by the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). In the year 1919-20 there were entered 4,437 birds, of which 823, or a percentage of 16.7, received certificates for 150 eggs and over per year, while there was a small percentage, 1.8, that got the advanced certificate for 225 eggs. All these birds had to lay eggs of at least two ounces in weight. The next year the number of birds entered was increased to 7,158, or an increase of 69 per cent. This year the number is 11,489, or 80 per cent of an ' increase, with 122 breeders. Does the minister intend to keep pace with the increase in these birds and follow up the work started by the late government, which is of a practical character and from which much benefit can be derived. If he does that, and it is increased to the extent that seems probable with the work started on the first of November next year, I should like to know if he has made any provision in his estimates for, say, doubling that line of work.

Yes. The work is well begun, and I think I cannot do better than continue it.

Replying to the hon. members for Dundas (Mr. Elliott) and Saltcoats (Mr. Sales) with respect to operating these farms on a commercial basis, that used to be discussed many years ago when these farms were first established. It was often contended, that even the experimental farm at Ottawa should show a profit, and the gentleman in charge of it at the time was occasioned a good deal of worry because he could not show a credit balance. Well, if it is a real experimental and demonstration farm, I do not think it ever will show a profit in dollars and cents; in fact, I do not see how it could be done. I need not point out to the committee that there are limitations which make it impossible to operate any of these farms on a commercial basis. No plan of farming will show a profit equal to the plan followed by the peasant proprietor. How is government operation of a farm to compare with private operation? How can you make a comparison from which it is possible to draw any intelligent conclusion? There will always be a certain amount of "frills" connected with government operation, no matter how carefully the farm may be managed. The average man looking on realizes that the manager of one of these experimental farms has the whole resources of the Dominion behind him, and if his crops are ruined by hail he is not "up against it". Therefore Mr. Average Man knows that the socalled commercial possibilities of such a farm would be of no avail to him. But we are entering upon a very practical age, and I shall be delighted if anyone will show me how our administration of any farm, whether at Rosthern, Scott or anywhere else, can be such as to combine benefit to the surrounding country and commercial profit.

I do not think the minister is taking the right interpretation. As to making an experimental farm a paying concern, I think there is no one so foolish as to even dream of such a thing. But it has been contended that some of this land that is being used for illustration and experimental purposes, but particularly for the former-we have not any illustration farms in Ontario, although I see there are thirty-three in Quebec and fifteen in the western provinces-could be utilized to demonstrate whether farming can be carried on at a profit. I do not think it is too much to ask that that should be done, in view of the fact that every dollar that has ever been asked for experimental purposes has been ungrudgingly voted. After all these years, and in view 
of the present very trying conditions for those engaged in agriculture, it is only fair that some object lessons should be available that would help them very considerably.

Knowing the conditions of farming, does not the minister think it would be a valuable thing to this country if what we have often contended could be abundantly demonstrated, namely, that farming can only be carried on profitably where we have a large amount of unpaid labour in the shape of women and children? We have made that assertion very frequently in our conventions, and I do not think it can be contradicted. We have been contending for some time, and we are trying to contend here, that under present conditions, and applying purely commercial principles, farming cannot be made a success. We are sometimes told that we are not businesslike in managing our farm affairs, and then we have the admission- and I believe it is a true admission-that the only man who can get the most out of farming is he who, like the peasant, gives himself wholly to it and has the assistance of his wife and children.
In the Committee on Agriculture to-day it was suggested that we should adopt dairying to a larger extent. Now, the only man who can make money out of dairying to-day is the man with a growing family whom he can exploit for a little time during their growing years and get their unpaid labour, and then they are driven from the farm. It would be a very good thing if that could be so clearly demonstrated on one of these farms that every one in Canada would understand the condition that agriculture is in.

There are some sections of our part of the country in which experimental or demonstration farms should be established in order to encourage the farmers. We have an experimental farm in the extreme west of the province, but it is some hundred miles from the shore counties, where there is a large area of great agricultural value. Farming is certainly the backbone of the country and it should be encouraged in every possible way. I would invite the minister's attention, therefore, to the case of my province. We are certainly not doing as well as we should, due to the fact that in some sections we have no encouragement whatever in the way of experimental farms. The illustration stations may be very good, but they serve only the

Supply-Experimental Farms
district immediately surrounding them, which is a very small area indeed. I would invite the minister to visit our part of the country and see the conditions with respect to farming there; he might be encouraged to do something in this connection. As I have intimated, the western part of the province is well looked after, but the eastern part, along the north shore, has been neglected. I would ask the minister to give this matter his serious consideration.

We are talking about experimental farms and demonstration farms, and I am rather afraid we are confusing the two. As I understand it, an experimental farm is a farm that will do many things that we are not expecting a profit from-I mean, directly, on that farm. The minister is justified, I think, in saying that he does not think it possible to put an experimental farm on a commercial basis. However, there is room for experimental farms, and, as some hon. members have said, there is room for demonstration. An experimental farm can demonstrate, more or less, but a demonstration farm would have to work along the line upon which the ordinary farmer carries on his actual work, and not very much experimenting could be done if it was hoped to make a profit. That is why the ordinary farmer expects the Dominion experimental farms to experiment; he does not want to have to do it himself. I support the idea of demonstration. We have had farms that we called demonstration farms in Alberta. I am not prepared to say just how much they have demonstrated, but I do not think they have made much profit. I do think they have made a mistake in going into the experimenting line; in my opinion, the purpose of a demonstration farm should be to demonstrate whether the methods we know of can be made to pay. The difference, then, between a demonstration farm and an experimental farm should be kept in mind. Some of the money spent in experimenting may be quite unproductive of results; in other cases, the results attained may be worth much more than the cost-that is the way we have to look at the work of an experimental farm. A demonstration farm which can make a success of the employment of scientific methods would be just as valuable to Canada to-day as an experimental farm. I would not expect it to make money, but if it can be done, I would like to see it done. But I would like
to see these two things, demonstration farms and experimental farms, looked at from a different standpoint, rather than one taking the place of the two.

The minister has
stated that the farm here at Ottawa, which is known as the Central Experimental Farm but which most of us call the Dominion Experimental Farm, is receiving more money than many of the others put together. I am quite willing to admit that I have a very high opinion of the work that is being done there. But it has occurred to most hon. members that owing to its geographical location this Central Experimental Farm is of equal value to Ontario and Quebec. I would not have mentioned this had it not been for the fact that in answer to a question put by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), the minister stated that outside of the Central Experimental Farm, which, as I have pointed out, serves equally the two old provinces, there are two smaller illustration or experimental farms in Ontario and thirty-eight in Quebec. I am sure that many of us have wondered what conditions gave rise to the necessity for a difference of thirty-six as between the two provinces.

A statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) a few minutes ago brought to my mind a subject to which I have given a great deal of thought. He said that in order to make farming pay it was necessary to have a peasant proprietorship. Too many people have been thinking along these lines and making statements of this kind. At present, high as wages are, those paid on the farm do not equal those paid in other industries. That is one of the reasons why it is difficult to get the very best class of labour on the farm-and it is only the very best class of labour that you want on the farm. Just as much skill is required on the farm as is necessary in any other industry; in many respects a great deal more skill is required. This matter of a man working a farm on a family basis, that is, using his family to work that farm without wages, does not tend to the ultimate good of the country. When the people are ignorant you can do that sort of thing and keep the boys at home. But when they begin to know anything at all; when the boys and the girls go to school, they soon learn where the highest wages are paid. Just as soon as they are old enough to

work they will leave the farm for higher wages. You will never have a successful immigration until you put the farming industry on a business footing where it can be made to pay. I saw in the paper the other day that the farmer and labour elements would never agree, because while labour wanted an eight-hour day, the farmer wanted a fifteen-hour day. I want to assure the hon. members of this House that the farmers do not want a fifteen-hour day, and the sooner they get down to an eight or a ten-hour day the better they will be pleased, and the better it will be for the country. You can never build up a country by asking a certain part of it to work for fourteen or sixteen hours a day, while the rest of the country is working a much shorter day. We hear a great deal nowadays of the baek-to-the-land movement, but the people who are advocating that are the ones who do not intend to go back to the land themselves. Just as soon as the Government can demonstrate that farming conducted on rational lines can be made to pay like any other business, even if a few extra hours have to be put in, then you will have immigrants coming to this country and they will stay here. But as long as you are content with saying that farming can only pay when it is conducted on the family basis, where the family work themselves without wages, you will never populate the country.

I do not think the
minister quite understood my suggestion. I quite appreciate that the experimental farms can do a good deal for every province in the breeding of live stock, poultry and that kind of thing, and experiments along that line carried on at the Central Farm here will be just as beneficial as experiments carried on in British Columbia. My suggestion was not to carry on a demonstration farm at all like an experimental farm, with expensive buildings and lands, but to take a graduate of the Agricultural College and put him on an ordinary farm, let him run it in a businesslike way, and simply go over his books at the end of the year, to see if it is possible for a capable man to make farming pay. All the expense the Government will be put to will be that of auditing his books. If you cannot show that a capable man can make farming pay, you will not get many immigrants coming to this country to farm. This Government, so far as I know, has never done anything to show that farming can be made to pay if carried on in a businesslike way.

I was encouraged to get on my feet when I heard the minister say that demonstration farms are of greatest benefit in the new territories. In my constituency, up in the Peace river district, we have a great new territory. I am not now asking for a demonstration farm, though some people up there have been asking for another one. The great difficulty there at the present time is freight rates. The Peace river country lies three to four hundred miles northwest of Edmonton. There is an experimental station at Beaver Lodge, and I believe that the gentleman who is in charge of that station is within measurable distance of proving that clover seed can be grown as a commercial proposition there. I believe he is badly handicapped for money this year, and I would ask the minister to take in consideration the needs of that part of the country. If the farmers can grow clover seed there on a commercial basis, the freight rates would not be nearly so oppressive as at the present time.

In reply to my
hon. friend who spoke of the large number of experimental farms in the province of Quebec, some thirty-eight in number, he made the mistake of bunching them all together. Thirty-three of these are just small illustration farms of twenty to twenty-five acres, and the farmer is paid about four dollars an acre for operating the farm. There is no overhead expenditure, no capital outlay, and few signs to indicate that it is a Dominion Government illustration farm. There are only four experimental farms in the province of Quebec, the other thirty-three being illustration stations that have been located where they were asked for. These farms in the province of Quebec have nearly all been organized during the last two or three years, and whatever credit may be coming to any one in connection therewith may be credited to the gentleman who preceded me in this office. I think some credit is coming to him, because these farms are doing a useful work. So let us get rid of the idea that there are thirty-eight experimental farms in the province of Quebec as against two in Ontario. The reason there are thirty-three illustration farms in the province of Quebec is that the people of that province have applied for them, while there have been very few applications, until quite recently, from the province of Ontario. Applications are beginning to come in now, however, and we anticipate locating a number of these farms in Ontario this summer.

Supply-Experimental Farms

There was nothing to indicate whether the farms in the list the minister read out were three acres or three hundred in extent, and that is how I got my impression that there were many more experimental farms in Quebec than in Ontario.

Quite right. Replying to my hon. friend who stated that a farm cannot be made to pay except as a self-contained unit operated by the members of the family, I think the past year has demonstrated that. As a matter of fact it was demonstrated in this province forty years ago when I was here. There were very few farms here then, more particularly in eastern Ontario, that were not operated as self-contained units, each supplying within itself a great deal of the raw material that went into the clothing of the family, as well as its food. Very few wages were paid out in this province forty years ago. In the western provinces as a result of the deflation of prices, on the one hand, and the high cost of farm implements and equipment, on the other, we have not been able to make it go under a system of hired labour. And if you had happened to go through the constituencies as I have-for example I passed through the constituency of the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales) just as harvest was beginning this year; the rust struck that country pretty severely and everybody was rushed on the farm-you would find families there with the boss-as we call him- on the binder, or a boy, maybe only thirteen or fourteen years of age, on the binder, and the parents and a number of children doing the stooking-a self contained unit. That may not be the ideal way to farm but that was the way in which the province of Ontario was largely pioneered-by self contained units.
When I said that the best way to get men on the farm to-day was to operate the farm on the principle of peasant proprietorship, I did not mean to imply the introduction of the peasant system as it exists in the older countries of Europe. The term "peasant proprietorship" is one that is used by economists or at least it was formerly used by writers on political economy in contradistinction to the system of owning and operating large farms. The principle of peasant proprietorship is that under which you own and operate your own farm and receive all the profits. The term I used is one employed by economists in describing the difference between small
farms-a self contained unit operated by the owner-and a large farm owned by a landlord and operated by a tenant.
Then the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) spoke of the eight hour a day system, meaning by that, I presume, working eight hours 'before dinner and eight hours after dinner. The eight hour day was introduced in the Old Country during the war and there was a great deal of money paid for overtime. I cannot hold out any hope, unless the Cost of operating in other respects is very substantially reduced that our hours will be very much lessened. After all, our rules are largely what we make them ourselves.

Would the minister advise that one of his little farms be conducted on an eight-hour basis just to demonstrate what beef, butter, eggs, and other foodstuffs would cost to produce on a farm run in that way, with time and one-half for over time?

I do not want to occupy too much of the time of the committee but several allusions have been made to the experimental farm in this city. I rise in order to pay my respects to that institution. Situated as it is with the acreage available and with the number of buildings it has occupying the land it can not very well be (conducted any differently from what it is at present. The branches conducted at the farm include health of animals, poultry, astronomical observatory, geodetic survey, and chemical laboratory. These all occupy space that really should be devoted to agricultural purposes. If I had my wish the minister should be placed in possession of sufficient funds to buy four hundred acres that immediately adjoin the farm. Then he would have an area of land that would not be cluttered up with buildings and would really be conducted as a farm should. At present the farm reseirtbles nothing so much as a small hamlet surrounded toy a nice lawn.
So much for the matter of the farm. There is a question I would like to ask the minister. Under Order in Council dealing with the Canadian standard for eggs, all Canadian eggs that are exported from this country must bear the Government inspection stamp on both ends of the case. I would like to know from the minister if it is the intention of the department to make the same regulation apply to eggs imported into this country. For instance, a large quantity of eggs enters Canada from the

United States and a very great quantity of highly flavoured1 eggs comes here from China. I would like to know from the minister if the same regulation should not apply to these importations that exists in the case of our Canadian exported eggs?
I will reply to my hon. friend's question when we1 come to take up the live stock vote.
I notice that further down the list there is a vote for cold storage warehouses.
We will come to that later; we are now dealing with the vote for experimental farms.

The minister has practically ignored my request for some explanation as to why there is an increase cf over $44,000 for experimental farms; he does not deem the request to be worthy of consideration. It appears, however, that he is dangling the greater part of this increase before somebody as likely to be expended for a new experimental farm; but he does not know and cannot inform the committee where it is going to be. It is a new experience, I think, for Parliament to be asked to vote such a sum as $44,000 without any information being vouchsafed as to what the money is intended for, and where it is to be expended. It is true the minister announced that he had in the back of his mind an idea that $30,000 was to go to the establishment of a farm somewhere in the northern part of British Columbia, but in saying this he ridicules the idea that there should be in an old province like Ontario any necessity for experimental farms. Under the circumstances I move seconded by Mr. Senn:
That item No. 41, being the estimate for experimental farms be reduced by J44.360.50, or the same amount that was voted in 1921.

Before the amendment is put let me say that there was no intention on my part to overlook my hon. friend's question. I have been trying to keep track of various questions that have been put and to give the desired information with respect to all of them. If I can be charged with anything it is
10 p.m. with being too detailed in my explanations. But I did inadvertently overlook that particular question of my hon. friend. However, I have the information here and there was no intention on my part to ignore it. There is no desire to conceal anything, because there is nothing to conceal. If there is an in-

crease in the vote it is because the experimental farm system is growing and when that is the case we require more money. The increase is intended to cover new work in plant pathology. That has reference to plant diseases, (including such diseases as rust; and if we spent $400,000 in that direction and secured a cure for rust it would be money well expended. I wish I could find the best available man in this continent for that work. If I could obtain the necessary salary to get that man and keep him, then we would be able to show a little better results than we are now able to produce. But, on account of being hobbled, handcuffed and hamstrung in connection with securing men and paying salaries, we have to take what we can get. This often means that we do not get results at all. There is an increase in wages. Wages have not gone down yet; they may go down; but when you have a good man on an experimental farm, you cannot reduce his wages. During all the time that I have been farming, I have not been able to say to an old, experienced hand: "I am going to reduce your salary." To say that would be an intimation to him to go, and he would take it in that way. It is not good policy to reduce the wages of good men. As a matter of fact, if I carried out one-half of the representations made to me and, sometimes, by hon. members, I would have four times as many men on the Central Experimental Farm; but the number is being kept down. A farmer has to have sufficient help for spring requirements, and in order to have men, he has to get them a little in advance. If he is sufficiently advanced in his work as he should be, these men will be waiting anxiously to jump to the land. I would imagine, if we sent a committee out to the Central Experimental Farm, they would find, at this particular time of the year, when the advent of spring is awaited, apparently too many men there; but in ten days or two weeks from now these men will be all busy at their respective duties.
There are, on that farm, some thirteen different divisions, and everyone of them is growing. If they were not growing and developing their usefulness, they should not be there; and if they are going to grow and develop and serve the country properly, the country must be prepared to pay for them. Instead of reducing this estimate, I should be apologizing for its being so small, because that is the way I feel about the matter. Since I had my civil government estimates under discus-
