sion, one of the best men in those thirteen divisions has left us simply because we are not paying him a sufficient salary to retain his services. I cannot give the committee his name, because his resignation is not public yet; but he is one of my best men in one of the most important branches. He is leaving us because he has an offer of $2,100 more than he was getting from us, with a prospect of an increase running up to-well, I will not say, but so much larger an amount than we are giving that we cannot hold him. If you put second and third class men on experimental farms and then equip those farms with what you like, you can spend a great deal of money and get very little result. But if you increase the value and quality of your r"key" men by twenty-five per cent, you will have results worth while, and whatever, within reason, it takes to get those "key" men, should be paid. A $6,000 or $8,000 man will do infinitely more and better work and give better service along the line of plant pathology than three, four or five men of a cheaper class whose salaries may aggregate no more than that of the one man. This is one of the reasons why, in my estimation, we are not getting along faster in the matter of plant pathology. We have not got the best men and these salaries will not secure the best men.
My information is that owing to the high cost, chemical supplies and apparatus in the division of chemistry have been allowed tq run down. As a matter of fact, nearly all these appropriations are smaller than were required in past years, and the result is that many of the farms have been handicapped in their work. It is true that the amount is larger than in the preceding year, but it is not enough to take care of the requirements of the farm. I have about half a page of reasons why this estimate is required, and the fact is that every one of these thirteen divisions is increasing its usefulness.
The hon. member for Carleton Mr. Garland) put a question with regard to poultry. At no time in the history of our country has poultry raising been so important as it is at the present. While we are importing Chinese eggs, we are exporting more high class eggs than we are importing of poor ones. We have a slight overage, and'the same thing is true with regard to butter. We are importing butter from New Zealand and Denmark, but we are exporting more than we are importing. There is plenty of room for
improvement, but you are not going to get improvement by putting cheap skates on experimental farms.

I was asking for an explanation with reference to the expenditure on farm labour, and the minister has not given it so far. He says: "There are a whole lot of boys there possibly standing around at this time of the year and you cannot get good farms by employing cheap skates." About $100,000 is being asked for under the head of civil government, for this experimental farm in addition to what I have been referring to. In 1920, the amount 'under the heading of Civil Government was $93,295, and it has been increased considerably since then. I do not know what the exact figure is at present; but there has been an increase of upwards of $40,000 for ordinary farm labourers on this farm, which is not a very extensive one. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Garland) says that it looks like a park. There is somewhere in the neighbourhood of four or five hundred acres in it. In the beginning of his remarks before six o'clock, the minister said that he thought that $30,000 of this amount would be expended1 for an experimental farm along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific in British Columbia. Now he says that it is for this and other experimental farms. Until we have some well-defined, clear statement, I think we would be voting money very recklessly in increasing this estimate to the amount asked for. I know some people will say: "Oh, you are voting to reduce the amount that the Government is ready to vote for agricultural purposes." If this was for the benefit of agriculture, or if it was the intention of the Government to see that there was to be an equitable distribution of the services of 'experimental farms in this country, the matter would be entirely different. But if some province has to do all this work itself and to pay for it, and, at the same time, to help to maintain farms in other provinces, that is absolutely unfair, and I am not going to vote in favour of such a proposition.
Amendment negatived.

the more some of these gentlemen want to spend. This vote is for entomology and the next, administration and enforcement of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act, shows an increase of $45,000. I think there are altogether too many fads being introduced. First we have an increase of $2,000 on entomology and then $45,000 on this next item alone, for a fad.

I am not thoroughly in sympathy with the remarks of the previous speaker inasmuch as there is ample room for the expenditure of a great part of this appropriation in a manner that would benefit a large section of the community. I do not know what explanation the minister may have for the increase in regard to the Destructive Insect and Pest Act vote, which the hon. member (Mr. Spence) has referred to, but I know where a large proportion of it might be applied with a possibility of great results. When we considered these estimates a few evenings ago some very interesting information was given to the House regarding this particular branch. We were told a good deal about what had been effected and what remained to be done in the way of combatting the enemies of field crops and standing timber. In my own constituency we are continually forced to conduct a warfare against fruit pests. We spray continuously during the spring and summer months to keep down the common pests of the orchard, such as green aphis, woolly aphis and oyster bark scale, which, if not brought under control, would put an end to all hope of profit from the orchard business in British Columbia. I must give the Department of Agriculture the credit which is due it for having co-operated efficiently and successfully, and along very well arranged lines, with the provincial government of British Columbia in the control of these pests. The minister has in his department a gentleman who has been almost of infinite service to us in British Columbia, although unfortunately he is no longer completely at the disposal of the province. I do not mind mentioning his name in the House; I refer to Mr. R. C. Treherne, than whom I doubt whether there is, in the whole range of the minister's officials, a more competent man. In fact, I think I should be safe in saying that there is not in the service of any other government a man better calculated to safeguard the interests of the public, in the particular line of activity he follows, than Mr. Treherne. There is an opportunity to greatly enlarge the activities 
of the department in connection with the most dangerous menace that threatens the fruit growers of Ontario, British Columbia, or any other section of the country where apples are produced. I refer to the codling moth. In one section of Washington, in spite of the fact that last year the district of Wenatchee expended $24 per acre in spraying to cope with that moth, the fruit growers lost a trifle over a million dollars in affected fruit. Hon. members can understand, in the light of such a fact, with what apprehension we view the danger of having that pest introduced into British Columbia. From 1905, when the pest was first noted in Victoria, up to last year, we have had fourteen outbreaks of this particular nuisance. Two-thirds of them were successfully coped with and the pest eradicated, but only for a while, because with refrigerator cars coming in from infested districts it is next to impossible to keep the pest out. I shall not enlarge on this subject but I could prove that a very considerable amount of money could be profitably spent in combatting this menace in Canada. I have in my hand a resolution forwarded to me from one of the Farmers' Institutes of the district from which I come, and a copy of which, I believe, has also been sent to the Department of Agriculture. After reciting in a general way the dangers and difficulties with which they have to contend the resolution goes on to say:
Be it resolved that we, the members of this Institute, go on record as being in favour of the enactment of any such legislation as will prohibit the 'importation of apples and pears from infected districts into Canadian territory.
This is a large question and one on which perhaps the minister is not prepared to give a definite statement this evening. But if possible I want to convey to the institute some answer which would give them an inkling of the intentions of the department. The minister is perfectly aware that other countries have passed legislation of this kind. Japan has a law keeping out fruit from countries infected with the codling moth. Australia has legislation which prohibits the importation of fruit from any country infected with fire blight, which is a far less serious menace than the codling moth. It cannot be successfully proven that fire blight can be propagated by mature fruit brought into the country, but there is no doubt in the world that our infestation in British Columbia came originally from pears brought from California. In other

Supply-Entomology
sections of which I have knowledge the infection came from apples brought from Ontario; and in spite of the constant vigilance of the provincial and Dominion officials it is one hard, long fight to keep the pest under control. I should be glad if the minister could give information as to whether he has answered the request from this Farmers' Institute, or has given it any consideration.

I have much
pleasure in giving the hon. member the information sought for. The first increase of $2,000 under the Entomological branch vote is intended to cover the purchase of additional apparatus and library supplies and also to provide for the employment of additional temporary employment during the summer, when the demand from the farmers for assistance in combatting insect pests is greatest. The member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould), and no doubt all other hon. gentlemen, will understand that. The insect pest, of course, is developed in the summer time, and during the last four or five years many parts of Canada have had a very much higher average temperature than in the previous five years, with the result that new varieties of insects have developed in the country that we never heard of formerly, or rarely if we did. The corn borer, for instance, has troubled us for some time; and although we have had the grasshopper in the West for some years, we never had it in Saskatchewan to any extent until within the last four or five years. The hot weather and dry season develop their own insects, and the further south you go towards the gulf the more insect pests you encounter, which shows that there is a relationship between heat and the number and variety of pests that are to be found in a place. In the Destructive Insect and Pest Act vote there is an increase of $45,000, an increase that is substantial and yet small when you appreciate the amount of work that is to be taken care of by the vote. The entomological vote is really divided into two sections, entomological and botanical. They are naturally more or less interwoven. They appear here in this form and have been so divided every year I suppose. They should be dovetailed into each other. The appropriation for this section last year was $108,000, the estimate for this year is $140,000, an increase of $32,000. Statutory increases in salaries account for $5,000, while the appointment of an increased number of seasonal officers, as well as additional permanent officers, takes $6,000 more. For providing for emergencies and for scouting for brown-tail moth, alfalfa weevil, corn-borer and grasshopper work an increase of $5,000 over last year will be required. It might be stated that an emergency arose during the current fiscal year in connection with the reappearance of the corn-borer in western Ontario. No emergency fund was provided last year, consequently a Governor General's Warrant had to be issued to cover the cost of this work. A further sum of $15,000 is estimated for the purchase of two vacuum sterilizers, one for the port of Montreal and one for Vancouver, these to be used for the sterilizing of plant material imported, to prevent the introduction of insect pests. That is the entomological section of this insect pest legislation.

Was part of this vote
used for the searching out and destruction of the spruce bud worm?

Yes, partly.
That comes more particularly under the Department of the Interior. They solicit the services of our men at times, and we do a certain amount of aeroplane scouting over the timber limits where this worm is at its worst. Then, acting on our reports, the lumberman can exploit his limits before the timber is destroyed. After the coniferous trees are partly killed by the bud worm the destruction is completed by the bark beetle. A good deal of this work could be taken care of. by the provincial authorities, and no doubt it is, and if greater precautions were taken to burn the debris after the lumberman completes his operations it would possibly prevent some of this trouble.

The money cannot be
better spent in assisting the provincial authorities, (because the preservation of our forests is of national importance. The destruction of our forests in New Brunswick by these insect pests is stated to represent thirty per cent of our forest wealth.

Recently a gentleman called on me and told me an alarming story about these insect pest invasions. He expressed the opinion that unless measurements are taken to protect our coniferous trees from the depredations of these pests we will not have any pulp-wood at the end of ten years.

That is right.

That is a very
serious statement, and I merely give it for what it is worth, but judging from the aeroplane scouting reports the depredations are very extensive and can be plainly seen from the air. The spruce bud worm is followed by the bark beetle, which completes the devastation, and if the lumbermen do not cut down the affected timber it is soon completely destroyed.
Now the botanical section. The appropriation for this section last year was $82,000, the estimate for this year is $95,000, an increase of $13,000. Of this amount $8,000 is intended to cover the extension of potato inspection work, at present carried on most extensively in the maritime provinces, to western Canada also. The remaining $5,000 increase is required to provide for the establishment of an additional plant pathological laboratory in Quebec, and to pay salaries of officers at the new laboratory at Summerland, B.C., not provided in last year's estimates. I had the pleasure of visiting some of the orchards at Nelson three or four years ago and was very much interested in their difficulties not only in connection with the codling moth-I do not think it was a trouble at that time-but in connection with many other kinds of pests that seem to be ready to attack almost every form of plant life whe,n you get a summer sufficiently warm to develop them. Here is the item:
Codling Moth-In the province of British Columbia the entomologist in charge of our activities has acted in an advisory capacity in field control operations, basing such operations on the knowledge resulting from life-history studies made from year to year by our officers. In the dry belt of British Columbia there are 1,165,369 apple and pear trees. The value of the apple crop alone to the growers for 1921 is estimated to be over $4,500,000. So far the codling moth has been controlled, but if it were allowed to become generally distributed, the losses from its ravages would in five years, including extra orchard control practices, would undoubtedly reach a total of $1,000,000. For the conducting of the control measures recommended, the Provincial Department of Agri-
culture appropriated $15,000 in 1921. Our officer in charge for British Columbia has completed an investigation which indicates that fifty per cent of the empty railroad cars entering British Columbia from eastern Canada and the United States, to be used for the carrying of fruit, contain either larvae or pupae of the insect, and to this source the chief infestations have been traced. A method of treating empty cars with live steam to destroy all insect life present has been tested during the year, and it is hoped this measure of control will become a recognized practice.
Mr. MaeKELVIE: One question in regard to the resolution I read. Has the minister given any consideration to placing an embargo against fruit coming in from infected districts?

We all have a feeling in the West that there are enough restrictions already against the importation of fruit. Out there we like to get a certain amount of fruit early in the season, and the more restrictions placed on importation the greater difficulty we will have in getting that fruit. But I think there should be another way of correcting that. There is no doubt that the infestations of the codling moth are due very largely to the carrying of infection by the ifruit in the cars. But there should be some method of checking it besides that suggested by my hon. friend-an embargo [DOT]against importation. Am I correct in understanding that that is the suggestion?
Mr. MaeKELVIE: It is suggested in the resolution placed in my hands by this institute for presentation to the minister-that is all.

If it became a
serious menace and that were the only solution, it would be well worth considering. A serious disease sometimes requires a serious remedy.
Mr. MaeKELVIE: Of course, if we had the guarantee that every refrigerator car or freight car which contained fruit coming into any orchard district would be thoroughly treated by some superheating [DOT]process which would destroy the larvae or cocoon, that would largely solve the difficulty.

I think the point taken toy the hon. member for Yale (Mr. MacKelvie) and emphasized in the resolution he speaks of is well worthy of consideration. There is real danger from having our orchards badly infested with the codling moth, and I do not think it is good policy to wait until the pest gets really
Supply-Entomology

bad in this country before taking measures to combat it. I would respectfully suggest to the minister that this matter be investigated very carefully indeed, and that every possible step be taken now to prevent a further infection of our orchards through fruit imported from other countries. The hon. member for Yale has pointed out that Australia and Japan have adopted measures to keep out the infected fruit. We anight carefully study those measures, and if they are really valuable and can be applied to our conditions, we should adopt them.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion on this vote for entomology, and I want to back up what has been said in regard to the necessity of protecting our orchards and our farms to the greatest possible extent. Last fall I went through southern Ontario and visited some of the sections where the corn-borer was at work, and the condition of some of the corn fields was appalling. The operations of this pest fiave reached the point where we cannot afford to relax our efforts to combat them, and we should foe ready with the money, if we have to get it by Supplementary Estimate, or by Governor General's Warrant, to meet the situation; otherwise our agriculture will receive a very bad setback. I want to endorse any work that is done along these lines.

If there is any fault to be found with the item under discussion it is not that suggested by the first hon. member who spoke to the item and who questioned what we were going to do with a paltry $28,000 in the face of the depredations of insects against the products of our farms, our orchards and our forests. The minister gave as one reason for the existence of these pests the excessively hot seasons which we have recently experienced. I would add to that another reason: since Confederation we have had in this House men of the same mind as the hon. member who first spoke on this item, and the result has been, as I have stated on the floor of this House on many occasions, that agriculture has been starved. We have had men who have had no appreciation of the value of agriculture, its necessities, or its enemies-and all the enemies of agriculture are not quadrupeds and centipedes; some of them are bipeds. That is what is the matter with this vote. As I have pointed out time and again in this House, agriculture has been acknowledged on political platforms as the
greatest thing in all Canada, as the backbone of the country, but when it comes to the floor of this House we find that "the greatest industry in Canada" is given the smallest vote of any department of government. A few years ago it was a paltry $3,000,000. On a previous occasion I pointed out in the House that, according to figures supplied by the Government themselves, the injury caused to agriculture alone was estimated at $125,000,000. According to information which came to my office, and to which, I think, the Minister of Agriculture also referred, it was estimated that over $1,000,000,000 was the extent of the loss to our forests through the depredations of flies and other insects upon our spruce trees. Then, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. MacKelvie), there have been the attacks of insect pests upon our fruit areas. Yet we have an hon. member standing up and condemning the Minister of Agriculture for asking for another $2,000 in the entomological branch. I hope that next year-though I do not hope the conditions will warrant it-in the interests of research work, and with a view to finding out means of preventing these depredations, this vote will be increased to $50,000. I hope the minister will have sufficient money to engage the services of real men, men of science, men who will work diligently along these lines. Now, I have indicated what is the matter in Canada at the present time; we have not had the proper perspective. It is false economy to cut down estimates of this kind, and I was pleased to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Yale and the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) in support of this item and against the criticisms of the hon. member who first spoke to the item. The appropriation is a very small one; it should be larger, so that iwe could have the kind of men who would discover means of combatting these pests. Did we not hear one of the ministers say a few nights ago that an increase of $400 by way of salary was necessary in his department because his department required men of greater expert knowledge than did the Department oTAgriculture? But no department requires men of greater knowledge, information and scientific attainments than the Department of Agriculture. I would support the minister therefore, in every honourable means to secure enough money to enable him to pay his employees salaries equal to those paid in other departments of government.



Supply-Cold Storage

I concur in the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria city (Mr. Tolmie) with regard to the operations of the corn-borer in southern Ontario. I myself come from that district, and I know that the corn-borer is a great menace to corn growing in that part of the province. I would like to ask the minister if his department has estimated the loss which has occurred through the depredations of that insect during the past year and what are the prospects of success in the employment of methods of eradication.

Item agreed to.
Agriculture-cold storage warehouses, $26,000.
Will the minister explain this item?
What does this vote cover precisely? Does it cover grants to cold storage warehouses?
Yes.
Where are they situated?

The committee
will remember that the Cold Storage Act was amended a few years ago to restrict the grants to municipal cold storage plants. That change means that not so much is paid out in subsidies, because the public are not taking advantage of the act as an assistance to a municipal proposition to the same extent that they would in the case of a co-operative enterprise. Before the act was amended, thirty per cent of the cost of erection was paid out by the government, but since the amendment only one or two plants have attempted to take advantage of it. It might be proper to consider at some time whether we should not revert to the old order.

Has the minister received any correspondence from farmers' associations in Nova Scotia with a view to the establishment of a cold storage plant in Nova Scotia, in Halifax, say, for the use of the farmers, for the storage of perishable goods shipped there for export?

I understand
that some representations have been made from that city with a view to having a government cold storage plant erected there, but nothing has been done as yet. We did contribute to the construction of a pre-cooling plant in the Annapolis valley for the storage of fruit before shipment.
"Mr. Gould.]
Will the minister be prepared to receive a deputation on this question at any time?
Yes; but I do not know that there is any provision for straight government constructipn.

How many of these government-aided cold storage plants are there in Canada, and what provision is made for the storage of small quantities of meat and fruit .by farmers in the localities where these plants are located?

Unfortunately,
just about the time we were beginning to speed up and make grants under the act, it was amended and made to apply only to municipal plants. The number of plants erected under this act from the beginning, in the Hon. Mr. Fisher's time, is thirty-four. I think the act was amended in 1917. The total refrigerating space is 5,244,258 feet, and the total cost $2,408,354. The farmers have the same rights in the matter of storage as any one else. I know that in Saskatchewan there is a special apartment allotted for the storing of meat, vegetables, fruit, butter and so forth, but particularly meat, by the farmers. There is a room set aside exclusively for that purpose at the plant at Melville so that the farmers can put in a quarter of beef or mutton and other farm produce. There is no regulation providing for that, but I think all the plants provide accommodation for that purpose. If at any time the operator desires to exclude farm produce, I think he could do so simply by pleading there was no room.
What is the charge for storing?

While the subsidy is in abeyance, the operators are usually pretty good and are not tempted to inflate the storage prices. At the opening of a new institution the rates are fixed between the government and the operator, and if any changes are required afterwards, that is done by negotiation. The rates have been changed from time to time. If the operating cost increases, inevitably the storage rates should increase. The weak point is that after the subsidy has been all paid there is difficulty in properly controlling the rates. I know that for some years after the subsidy has been paid the different plants submit new schedules of rates to the department, recognizing its right to oversee the rates, but in law there

Supply-Cold Storage
is some doubt whether we have the right to compel them not to exceed certain rates.
Under the law, have not the rates to receive the approval of the government?
Yes.

The cold storage plants have been a great blessing in many ways, but I would point out to the minister that there has been considerable anxiety in certain of our large industrial centres regarding the operation of some of our cold storage warehouses. The fault found with those plants that are run by large corporations, who store goods in these warehouses for sale later, is that the foodstuffs are kept for too long a period. That has the effect of enhancing the price. They wait until the particular products they are handling, such as eggs, meats and other foods, become scarce throughout the country and then unload them at a higher price. Has the department any regulations governing these particular aspects of cold storage?
I notice that an hon. gentleman in another House has introduced a bill regarding the matter.
Yes in the Senate.

A bill was introduced, I think, in the session of 1913, but it received scant courtesy from the House at that time. There is an undoubted grievance in connection with cold storage warehouses. For example, a cold storage warehouse in the city of Montreal a few years ago got a corner on the egg market. Eggs were held up until they became a scarce commodity and then unloaded on the public at a very high rate. That is the thing the people in industrial centres have a right to protest against. There is no doubt in the world that cold storage plants have been a great benefit, but when such plants are subsidized by public money the Government should exercise sufficient control over them as to render impossible the things of which I have complained.
Might I ask my hon. friend if the plant to which he refers was a subsidized plant?
I so understood, but I am not in a position to say definitely.
I shall be very pleased to look into the matter.
In respect to what my hon. friend from Cape Breton has stated, my recollection is that there is a cold storage warehouse under control of the Harbour Commissioners at Montreal.
Yes, a very good one.
A very good one. I took a good deal of pride in that. It was originated when I was at the head of the Department of Agriculture.
I think my hon. friend borrowed the idea from Saskatchewan.

Yes, that is where a great many good things come from and some indifferent things also. But in respect of the cold storage warehouse which is under the control of the Harbour Commissioners in Montreal, is that not available for public storage?

Yes.
Supply-Cold Storage

If it is available for public storage, that should get over the difficulty raised by my hon. friend from Cape Breton, because any merchant or wholesale man would be at liberty to purchase his eggs and have them stored in this public cold storage warehouse and shipped out at his disposal. Is that correct?

Yes. They are just beginning to use that cold storage warehouse now. I have had inquiries from Regina in regard to the rates they were charging in Montreal and from that fact I know the warehouse is being used. There is a certain amount of competition, and keen competition where there is a large number of these plants and I want to congratulate the hon. member (Mr. Crerar) in connection with that cold storage warehouse. It would have been a great service to the country if it had been built a few years sooner, especially during the war.

What action has been
taken in the past to protect the public against impure foodstuffs? Do inspectors visit these plants regularly to see that the food commodities are in good condition? Because in the city of Montreal as well as in the much vaunted western Canada hundreds of tons of chickens were taken from cold storage warehouses and destroyed on account of being unfit for human food. What measures are taken to guarantee the public that they will get pure food from these plants?

I may say that
when a cold storage plant is subsidized it has to be ok'd by the department and during the process of construction a constant inspection is maintained to see that the plans and specifications are lived up to. So long as the subsidy, or any portion of it, remains unpaid we can maintain inspection. But there is no regular inspection and we have not the control that we would have if such an inspection were carried out. There certainly is a weakness there which should be corrected somehow. I have not as yet, had the necessary time to look into this matter and determine the extent to which an inspection might be carried on.

There is a Food Inspection Act under which, for example, government inspectors visit different stores from which they take samples of maple sugar and have them analyzed in order to determine whether they conform to a certain standard of purity. If the minister has power to do that, why has he not the power to carry out a regular inspection of

cold storage plants in order to see that the food products stored therein are fit for human consumption?

I think that is
a matter that would devolve on the provincial and Dominion boards of health.

The inspection to
which I refer is, I think, practically carried out by the federal authorities.

It is a matter
under the control of the Dominion or provincial Department of Health.

Is that an opinion
given by the Department of Justice in writing?

I think it is an
opinion given in writing.

I think the minister
should bring that information down to the House.

I will do so if
my hon. friend will call for a return.

I would like to suggest
that as it is now eleven o'clock and as a number of hon. members on this side who would like to take part in the discussion of these items are not present, the com-mitte should rise.

Before the House adjourns, if I might be permitted with the consent of the House, I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that, when the House adjourns over the Easter recess, we adjourn from Tuesday evening instead of from Wednesday evening. As we sit for only three hours on Wednesday, that is all we shall gain by sitting on that date. I find that some hon. gentlemen from the prairie provinces desire to avail themselves of the Easter recess to go home. If they leave on Tuesday night, as I understand the matter, their days throughout the rest of the week are charged up against them. If my hon, friend would agree to change the motion to read that we adjourn from Tuesday evening instead of from Wednesday, many members on this side of the House would appreciate that very much.

Grand Trunk Arbitration
Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister: The Government has, in this matter, only one wish, and that is to consult the convenience of the members. I had heard that a number of the members desired that the House should adjourn on Tuesday, and I take it that it is the general wish of the members that the suggestion just made by my hon. friend be acted upon. If so, I shall have pleasure, at the dose of to-night's sitting, in giving notice that, when we adjourn on Tuesday next, the House shall stand adjourned until the following Tuesday.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King, the House adjourned at 11.05 p.m.
